one_line: High-norm outlier tokens in CLIP-style ViTs, not decoder design, are the primary bottleneck for training-free open-vocabulary segmentation.
problem: Zero-shot segmentation from frozen VLM patch features is noisy, and the field responds mostly with increasingly elaborate decoding heuristics rather than asking why the raw similarity maps are corrupted.
core_hypothesis: A small set of high-norm 'attention sink' patch tokens carry global rather than local information and dominate patch-text similarity maps; suppressing or imputing them recovers most of the quality currently attributed to sophisticated training-free decoders.
falsifiable_prediction: On the same frozen backbone, masking or imputing the highest-norm patch tokens before computing patch-text similarity will improve zero-shot segmentation quality by at least as much as switching between popular training-free decoding heuristics.
why_important: If true, effort should shift from decoder engineering to token-statistics hygiene, a cheap fix applicable to every frozen-backbone dense pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Outlier tokens are discussed for self-supervised ViTs and interpretability, but a controlled causal comparison of outlier suppression against decoder variants specifically for open-vocabulary segmentation may be missing; not verified against the literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one frozen CLIP-style ViT; evaluate zero-shot segmentation with (a) vanilla patch-text similarity, (b) the same plus outlier-token suppression, (c) two established training-free decoding variants, on one standard benchmark with identical prompts.
main_risk: Outlier suppression and decoder heuristics may fix the same underlying failure, making gains non-additive and the attribution ambiguous.
community_default_belief: CLIP-style models localize poorly because image-level contrastive training provides essentially no spatial signal, so heavy decoding machinery is required.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The spatial signal may be present but masked by a handful of pathological tokens, meaning the objective is less at fault than the token statistics it induces.
fastest_falsification: A single afternoon-scale run: plot patch-norm histograms, ablate top-norm tokens, and re-score similarity maps on a few hundred images.

one_line: VLM patch embeddings encode global image gist more than local patch content, and this 'patch leakage' bounds dense transfer.
problem: Dense adaptation methods assume patch embeddings primarily describe their own receptive field, but contrastive training only ever supervises a pooled global vector.
core_hypothesis: In contrastively trained VLMs, a linear probe can decode the whole-image class from a single patch embedding more accurately than that patch's own local content, and the ratio of global-to-local decodability predicts dense transfer quality across backbones.
falsifiable_prediction: Patch-transplant experiments (pasting a patch's embedding context from another image) will change patch-text similarity more than changing the patch's own pixels, for contrastive VLMs but not for dense-supervised baselines.
why_important: It would give a measurable pretraining-time quantity that predicts dense usefulness, guiding backbone selection before any finetuning.
why_possibly_novel: Global information leakage into patch tokens has been observed qualitatively; using it as a quantitative predictor of dense transfer across VLM backbones may be unexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two or three frozen backbones, train linear probes decoding (a) local patch label and (b) global image label from single patch embeddings; correlate the local/global decodability ratio with zero-shot segmentation quality of the same backbones.
main_risk: Local and global decodability may be too correlated across available backbones to separate, requiring interventional rather than observational comparisons.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Pooled-objective gradients still differentiate patches through attention, so locality may survive more than the leakage story implies.
community_default_belief: Patch tokens of ViTs are treated as local descriptors roughly aligned with their spatial position, which is why frozen-feature segmentation is expected to work at all.
fastest_falsification: Patch-swap probing on a few hundred images with one frozen backbone and one linear probe, runnable in hours.

one_line: For some classes, VLM similarity maps peak on co-occurring background rather than the object, making errors anti-correlated with the object, not random.
problem: Open-vocabulary segmentation errors are usually reported as aggregate IoU, hiding a qualitative failure where the model grounds a word to its typical context instead of the object.
core_hypothesis: Contrastive alignment binds words to whole scenes, so for context-dependent classes the patch-text similarity is systematically higher on the co-occurring background; a per-class 'anti-grounding' score is stable across datasets and predicts which classes benefit from context-suppression fixes.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class correlation between similarity maps and ground-truth masks will be significantly negative for an identifiable subset of classes, and that subset will replicate across at least two datasets.
why_important: Anti-grounded classes need a different fix (context suppression) than weakly grounded classes (better features), so lumping them together wastes method development.
why_possibly_novel: Background-attention anecdotes exist, but a systematic per-class anti-grounding taxonomy with cross-dataset replication may not; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class spatial correlation between raw patch-text similarity and ground-truth masks on two segmentation datasets with a shared frozen backbone; test whether the anti-grounded class set replicates.
main_risk: Anti-grounding may be an artifact of one backbone family rather than a general property of contrastive VLMs.
community_default_belief: Zero-shot similarity maps are treated as noisy-but-centered estimates of object location, justifying refinement-style decoders.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the maps are systematically inverted for some classes, refinement decoders sharpen the wrong region and can never fix those classes.
fastest_falsification: One frozen backbone, one dataset pass computing per-class map-mask correlations; negative-correlation classes are immediately visible.

one_line: Dense-relevant information in VLM encoders peaks at intermediate layers, and layer selection matters more than adapter architecture for dense transfer.
problem: Most dense adaptation work bolts decoders onto the final layer of frozen VLMs, implicitly assuming the last layer is the most informative for pixels.
core_hypothesis: The final layers of contrastive VLMs specialize toward the global alignment objective and discard spatial detail, so a probing curve over depth is non-monotonic for dense tasks; choosing the best intermediate layer yields larger gains than switching among adapter designs applied to the final layer.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise linear probing for segmentation on a frozen VLM will show an intermediate-depth peak, and the best-layer probe will outperform at least two adapter variants attached to the final layer at matched trainable parameters.
why_important: A free, architecture-agnostic gain for every frozen-VLM dense pipeline, and a reusable diagnostic for backbone comparison.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-wise analyses exist for classification and self-supervised models; a controlled layer-versus-adapter tradeoff study for VLM dense prediction may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe every fourth layer of one frozen VLM with an identical lightweight segmentation head; compare the best intermediate layer against final-layer adapters at matched parameter count on one benchmark.
main_risk: The effect size may be backbone-specific, with modern VLMs trained with auxiliary dense losses showing flat curves.
community_default_belief: The final representation of a strong VLM is the right substrate for downstream heads, as it is for classification.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Classification benefits from exactly the invariances that dense prediction must undo, and the last layers are where those invariances are enforced hardest.
fastest_falsification: Layer-probing sweep with a frozen backbone and a linear head, a few GPU-hours.

one_line: Patch-embedding norms in VLMs encode class-agnostic objectness well enough to rival learned mask-proposal stages.
problem: Open-vocabulary pipelines typically train a proposal or mask-generator stage, adding cost and a closed-world bias inherited from proposal training data.
core_hypothesis: Because contrastive training pushes informative regions to higher feature magnitude, simple functions of patch norm (possibly after outlier removal) provide objectness maps whose proposal recall approaches trained proposal networks, without any dense supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: Thresholded, connected-component proposals derived from patch-norm maps of a frozen VLM will reach a substantial fraction of the proposal recall of a trained class-agnostic proposal network on a held-out dataset, especially for categories absent from proposal training data.
why_important: Would remove a trained component that silently reintroduces closed-vocabulary bias into 'open-vocabulary' systems.
why_possibly_novel: Feature norms are used for outlier analysis and saliency, but their use as a competitive zero-training proposal mechanism benchmarked against trained proposal stages may be untested; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract patch-norm maps from one frozen VLM, derive proposals via thresholding and connected components, and compare average recall against one trained class-agnostic proposal model on one dataset, stratified by whether categories appeared in proposal training.
main_risk: Norm maps may capture texture saliency rather than objectness, inflating recall on cluttered textures and failing on smooth objects.
community_default_belief: A learned proposal stage is necessary because raw VLM features cannot delineate object extents.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The delineation signal may already exist in feature magnitude statistics; it has simply never been evaluated as a proposal mechanism on equal footing.
fastest_falsification: Norm-map extraction plus connected components on a validation split, comparable within a day.

one_line: Contrastive pretraining buys translation invariance at the price of boundary precision, and the deficit is objective-specific rather than resolution-specific.
problem: VLM-based segmenters are often reported to have soft, imprecise boundaries, usually blamed on low input resolution or patch size.
core_hypothesis: In-batch contrastive objectives reward local translation invariance, measurably blurring boundary-adjacent feature transitions; at matched resolution and patch size, contrastive VLMs will show a larger boundary-versus-interior quality gap than dense-supervised or reconstruction-pretrained models.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing backbones matched for architecture, resolution, and patch size but differing in pretraining objective, the ratio of boundary F-score to interior IoU will be systematically lower for contrastive VLMs.
why_important: It tells us whether boundary quality can be fixed with upsampling tricks or requires changing the pretraining objective itself.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary quality is usually treated as a decoder or resolution problem; attributing it causally to the contrastive objective via matched-backbone comparisons may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe three matched backbones (contrastive, masked-reconstruction, dense-supervised) with identical frozen-feature segmentation heads; decompose quality into boundary and interior components on one benchmark.
main_risk: Truly matched backbones across objectives are scarce, and confounds from training data may swamp the objective effect.
community_default_belief: Boundary softness in VLM segmentation is an artifact of patch size and input resolution that will disappear with higher-resolution training.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If invariance is baked into features by the objective, resolution scaling sharpens the grid, not the representation, and the gap persists.
fastest_falsification: Boundary/interior metric decomposition on existing frozen-feature results across two backbones, doable without new training.

one_line: Patch-level text alignment in VLMs emerges discontinuously with scale, unlike smoothly improving image-level alignment.
problem: Dense transfer results are usually reported at one model scale, and practitioners extrapolate as if dense ability scales like classification.
core_hypothesis: Zero-shot dense metrics across a family of checkpoints spanning model and data scale will show threshold-like emergence (near-flat then rapid rise), whereas zero-shot classification improves smoothly, implying dense usefulness cannot be predicted from classification-scale curves.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a public family of contrastive checkpoints, the scale-versus-performance curve for training-free segmentation will exhibit a significantly sharper transition than the corresponding classification curve.
why_important: Determines whether small-scale dense prototyping is informative and whether dense capability should gate pretraining-scale decisions.
why_possibly_novel: Emergence debates focus on LLM tasks and VQA; a controlled emergence analysis for dense patch-text alignment may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate training-free segmentation and zero-shot classification for every checkpoint in one public scale family under identical prompts; compare curve shapes with a fitted transition-sharpness statistic.
main_risk: Apparent emergence may be a metric artifact (thresholded IoU) rather than a representational transition, requiring continuous-metric controls.
community_default_belief: Dense capability of VLMs improves gradually with scale, mirroring classification, so bigger is predictably better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Patch-level alignment is an unsupervised byproduct, not an optimized objective, and byproducts can appear abruptly once capacity frees up.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only sweep over an existing checkpoint family on one segmentation benchmark.

one_line: Anisotropy of VLM patch-feature space, not prompt quality, limits zero-shot dense prediction, and simple whitening beats prompt ensembling.
problem: Practitioners invest heavily in prompt ensembles and templates to squeeze quality from patch-text similarity, treating the feature geometry as fixed.
core_hypothesis: VLM patch embeddings occupy a narrow anisotropic cone that compresses class-discriminative directions; whitening patch features with statistics from unlabeled images enlarges effective angular separation and improves zero-shot segmentation more than prompt ensembling does.
falsifiable_prediction: In a two-by-two ablation (whitening on/off, prompt ensembling on/off), whitening will contribute a larger improvement than ensembling, and their combination will be sub-additive.
why_important: A training-free, prompt-free correction applicable to any frozen VLM, and evidence that many prompt tricks are workarounds for geometry, not semantics.
why_possibly_novel: Anisotropy is well studied for sentence embeddings; its causal role in dense visual-text similarity and the whitening-versus-ensembling comparison may be unexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate patch-feature covariance on unlabeled images, apply whitening, and run the two-by-two ablation on one benchmark with a fixed backbone.
main_risk: Whitening statistics may be dataset-specific, silently reintroducing a domain-adaptation step that inflates apparent gains.
community_default_belief: Prompt engineering and ensembling are the main free levers for improving zero-shot dense performance from frozen VLMs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If ensembling mostly averages out anisotropy noise, fixing the geometry directly is the primary correction and prompts are secondary.
fastest_falsification: Covariance estimation plus re-scoring on a validation split, a few hours with cached features.

one_line: Open-vocabulary segmentation rankings are unstable under synonym substitution of class names, revealing lexical rather than semantic grounding.
problem: Benchmarks fix one canonical name per class, so reported scores conflate visual grounding ability with luck in matching the pretraining-frequent name.
core_hypothesis: Replacing class names with common synonyms changes per-class IoU by more than typical method-to-method differences, and method rankings computed under different synonym choices disagree materially.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a curated synonym set, the rank correlation of method leaderboards between synonym conditions will be substantially below one, and per-class score swings will exceed the average published gap between competing methods.
why_important: If rankings depend on word choice, the field is partly optimizing lexical alignment rather than dense visual understanding, and benchmark conclusions are fragile.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is known for classification; quantifying leaderboard instability under synonyms for dense tasks may be undone; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build synonym lists for one benchmark's classes, re-evaluate three published open-vocabulary segmenters under each synonym condition, and compute cross-condition rank correlations.
main_risk: Synonyms are not perfectly meaning-preserving, so some score changes reflect genuine semantic shifts rather than lexical fragility.
community_default_belief: Open-vocabulary results measure the ability to segment concepts, with the specific class string being an implementation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive text encoders are trained on surface forms, so the string is not a detail: it selects which slice of pretraining distribution the model retrieves.
fastest_falsification: Re-scoring cached predictions is impossible (text changes the prediction), but inference-only re-runs on a subset of classes take under a day.

one_line: Prompt templates inherited from classification are systematically suboptimal for dense prediction, and the optimal template differs by class type.
problem: Dense pipelines reuse 'a photo of a {}' style templates tuned for image-level classification without asking whether region-level matching needs different language.
core_hypothesis: Templates describing regions, materials, or partial views align better with patch-level features than whole-image templates, and the gap is larger for stuff classes than thing classes, because captions describe whole scenes while patches depict parts.
falsifiable_prediction: A region-oriented template set will outperform classification templates for stuff classes by a larger margin than for thing classes, consistently across two backbones.
why_important: A zero-cost improvement and a diagnostic for how patch features relate to caption language, informing prompt design beyond folklore.
why_possibly_novel: Template studies exist for classification; a systematic thing-versus-stuff template interaction analysis for dense tasks may not; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three template families (whole-image, region-oriented, bare-name) on one segmentation benchmark split into thing and stuff classes, with two frozen backbones.
main_risk: Template effects may be small relative to per-class variance, requiring many classes for statistical power.
community_default_belief: Good classification templates are good dense templates, so template design is a solved detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Patch embeddings are matched against text describing whole images during pretraining only implicitly; the effective 'language of patches' may differ from the language of photos.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only template sweep on cached image features, hours of compute.

one_line: The stuff-class performance gap in open-vocabulary segmentation is primarily a text-encoder deficiency, not a vision-feature deficiency.
problem: Open-vocabulary segmenters consistently underperform on amorphous 'stuff' categories, and the blame is placed on visual features lacking texture-region support.
core_hypothesis: Text encoders trained on object-centric captions represent mass nouns (grass, pavement, water) in a degenerate region of embedding space; substituting better text-side representations while freezing vision features closes a large fraction of the stuff-thing gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Replacing class-name embeddings for stuff classes with embeddings derived from richer descriptions or a stronger text model (vision tower fixed) will improve stuff IoU disproportionately compared to applying the same substitution to thing classes.
why_important: It redirects the fix toward text-side interventions, which are vastly cheaper than retraining vision towers for dense tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Stuff-thing gaps are documented; causally attributing them to the text side via one-sided substitution experiments may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark, swap in three alternative text embeddings per class (rich description, definition sentence, stronger text encoder mapped into the joint space) and measure stuff-versus-thing improvement asymmetry.
main_risk: Mapping a stronger text encoder into the joint space introduces its own error, confounding the attribution.
community_default_belief: Stuff classes are hard because their visual extent is ambiguous and texture-like, a vision-side problem.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Vision features for textures are actually plentiful; what may be missing is a text anchor that points at them, since captions rarely name background stuff.
fastest_falsification: Text-embedding substitution requires no retraining; a day of inference on one benchmark.

one_line: Fine-grained open-vocabulary dense prediction collapses to basic-level categories because hypernym similarity dominates class-name embeddings.
problem: As vocabularies grow fine-grained (breeds, species, product types), dense predictions degrade in ways not explained by visual similarity alone.
core_hypothesis: Text embeddings of fine-grained names are dominated by their hypernym component, so patch similarities barely distinguish siblings; confusion mass flows toward basic-level categories beyond what visual confusability predicts.
falsifiable_prediction: In nested-vocabulary evaluation, the fraction of errors going to hypernyms and co-hyponyms will exceed a visual-similarity-matched baseline, and text-embedding sibling separation will predict per-class degradation better than visual sibling separation.
why_important: Fine-grained dense recognition is the practical promise of open vocabulary; if text geometry caps it, the fix lies in text-side contrast, not more segmentation data.
why_possibly_novel: Hierarchy effects are studied for classification; a dense-prediction error-flow analysis with matched visual controls may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a three-level nested vocabulary for one dataset, evaluate a fixed segmenter at each level, and decompose confusions against visual and textual sibling-similarity baselines.
main_risk: Fine-grained ground truth in segmentation datasets is scarce and noisy, limiting the reliable class set.
community_default_belief: Fine-grained failure is a data problem: models simply have not seen enough labeled examples of rare fine categories.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If sibling names are nearly collinear in text space, no amount of visual data fixes discrimination that the query representation cannot express.
fastest_falsification: Measure pairwise text-embedding similarities of sibling class names versus cross-family names; near-collinearity is checkable in minutes, with the dense confirmation in a day.

one_line: Tokenization length of a class name is an independent predictor of its open-vocabulary dense performance, beyond frequency and visual difficulty.
problem: Per-class performance analyses attribute variation to visual factors or data frequency, ignoring that the tokenizer fragments some names into many rare subwords.
core_hypothesis: Names splitting into more subword tokens produce noisier text embeddings, and this measurably reduces dense performance after controlling for name frequency and object size; single-token aliases recover part of the loss.
falsifiable_prediction: In a cross-class regression, token count will carry significant negative weight on per-class IoU after frequency and size controls, and replacing multi-token names with equally rare single-token aliases will differentially help the fragmented classes.
why_important: It exposes a hidden, fixable interface artifact: vocabulary construction and alias selection become cheap performance levers.
why_possibly_novel: Tokenizer effects are studied for LLM arithmetic and multilingual text; connecting them to dense visual grounding may be unexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Regress per-class dense scores on token count, log frequency proxy, and mean object size across two benchmarks; then run the alias-substitution intervention on the most fragmented classes.
main_risk: Token count correlates with morphological complexity and rarity in ways controls may not fully capture.
community_default_belief: The tokenizer is a transparent plumbing detail; what matters is the concept the name denotes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive text encoders build name embeddings compositionally from subwords, so fragmentation directly perturbs the query vector that dense matching depends on.
fastest_falsification: The regression uses only existing per-class results plus tokenizer statistics; computable in an afternoon.

one_line: Prompt ensembling gains for dense prediction are mostly a workaround for embedding anisotropy and vanish after feature whitening.
problem: Prompt ensembling is treated as capturing semantic diversity, but nobody has separated that from its purely geometric averaging effect.
core_hypothesis: Averaging template embeddings mainly cancels a shared anisotropic bias direction; once patch and text features are whitened, the marginal benefit of ensembling over a single good template becomes negligible for dense tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: The improvement from ensembling measured after whitening will be a small fraction of the improvement measured before whitening, consistently across backbones.
why_important: Clarifies what prompt engineering actually does, and replaces per-task template curation with a one-time geometric correction.
why_possibly_novel: Ensembling and anisotropy are separately known; testing their interaction in the dense setting may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two-by-two design (whitening x ensembling) on one segmentation benchmark with two frozen backbones and a fixed template pool.
main_risk: Some templates genuinely alter semantics (materials, parts), so a residual ensembling gain may persist and muddy the interpretation.
community_default_belief: Prompt ensembles help because different templates capture complementary meanings of the class.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the dominant effect were semantic, gains would survive whitening; if geometric, they should collapse, which is exactly what the experiment separates.
fastest_falsification: All conditions are inference-only re-scoring of cached features; runnable in a day.

one_line: Learned 'background' embeddings in open-vocabulary segmentation do not transfer across vocabularies, making rejection quality an unmeasured failure mode.
problem: Open-vocabulary segmenters need to label pixels belonging to none of the queried classes, and common solutions learn a background embedding on one training vocabulary.
core_hypothesis: The learned background embedding encodes 'not in my training vocabulary' rather than 'not in the current query set', so rejection quality collapses when the deployed vocabulary differs from the training one, in either direction (larger or smaller).
falsifiable_prediction: Holding the model fixed and varying only the query vocabulary, false-positive rate on truly-background pixels will change dramatically and systematically with vocabulary overlap, whereas an ideal rejection mechanism would be stable.
why_important: Real deployments change vocabularies constantly; a rejection mechanism tied to training vocabulary silently breaks the core promise of open-vocabulary systems.
why_possibly_novel: Background handling is discussed per-method; a cross-vocabulary rejection-transfer evaluation protocol may not exist; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one trained open-vocabulary segmenter; evaluate background precision/recall under nested, disjoint, and superset query vocabularies on the same images.
main_risk: Disentangling rejection failure from ordinary classification error requires careful pixel-level bookkeeping of which classes are queryable.
community_default_belief: Background is a nuisance class handled adequately by a learned embedding or a threshold, orthogonal to open-vocabulary capability.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rejection is the complement of the query set, so it is definitionally vocabulary-dependent; a static learned embedding cannot represent a moving complement.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only vocabulary manipulation on an existing checkpoint, one day.

one_line: Bag-of-words behavior of VLM text encoders imposes a hard ceiling on dense tasks requiring syntax, measurable by word-order perturbation invariance.
problem: Referring segmentation and relation-conditioned detection assume the text encoder distinguishes 'dog chasing cat' from 'cat chasing dog', which contrastive encoders are widely suspected not to do.
core_hypothesis: For dense systems built on contrastive text towers, output masks are largely invariant to meaning-changing word-order permutations of the query, and the degree of this invariance predicts the system's failure rate on relation-critical referring expressions.
falsifiable_prediction: Shuffling or role-swapping words in referring expressions will change predicted masks far less than it changes meaning, and per-model order-sensitivity will correlate with relation-subset accuracy across systems.
why_important: It identifies which dense failures are unfixable at the decoder level and require replacing or augmenting the text tower.
why_possibly_novel: Order-insensitivity is established for image-text retrieval; propagating it quantitatively to dense outputs and using it as a predictive diagnostic may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For three referring-segmentation systems, measure mask change (IoU between original and perturbed-prompt outputs) under role-swap perturbations, and correlate with accuracy on relation-dependent subsets.
main_risk: Some systems inject the query into cross-attention at multiple stages, so invariance may vary by architecture in ways that complicate a single diagnostic.
community_default_belief: Referring segmentation failures stem from visual grounding difficulty, with the language side assumed adequate for short expressions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the query embedding cannot represent role bindings, the vision side never receives the information, no matter how good the grounding machinery is.
fastest_falsification: Prompt-perturbation battery on one system, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Dense grounding of spatial relations is driven by object priors, not relations: predictions barely change when the stated relation is inverted.
problem: Systems are credited with understanding 'the cup left of the laptop' when they may only be detecting 'cup' and exploiting scene statistics.
core_hypothesis: For VLM-based referring segmentation, swapping the relation word ('left of' to 'right of') changes the predicted mask in only a small minority of cases where the swap should change the referent, and success cases are explained by single-candidate scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes containing two same-category candidates disambiguated only by a spatial relation, accuracy will drop to near coin-flip, while reported benchmark accuracy stays high because such scenes are rare in benchmarks.
why_important: Spatial language is the main tool humans use to disambiguate references; if it is ignored, interactive dense systems fail exactly when users need them.
why_possibly_novel: Relation-insensitivity is suspected in VQA; a controlled two-candidate dense evaluation isolating relation use may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or synthesize scenes with two identical-category objects; evaluate paired prompts differing only in the relation word; report the fraction of prediction flips.
main_risk: Synthetic two-candidate scenes may be out-of-distribution in ways that depress performance for reasons other than relational failure.
community_default_belief: High referring-benchmark scores indicate models integrate spatial language with vision.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Benchmarks are dominated by expressions where the head noun alone identifies the referent, so relation understanding is never actually tested.
fastest_falsification: A hundred curated two-candidate images with paired prompts, evaluated on one public model in a day.

one_line: VLM dense grounding defaults to viewer-centric frames of reference and cannot switch to object-centric frames on request.
problem: Expressions like 'to the dog's left' require an object-centric frame; models are never evaluated on frame-of-reference control.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictions for object-centric spatial expressions match viewer-centric interpretations at well above chance, indicating the frame is hard-coded by dataset statistics rather than parsed from language; mirrored-image tests expose the bias cleanly.
falsifiable_prediction: On stimuli where viewer-centric and object-centric readings pick different referents, models will choose the viewer-centric referent in the large majority of cases regardless of the linguistic frame marker.
why_important: Robotics and assistive applications routinely use object- and speaker-centric frames; a hidden viewer-centric default causes confident, systematic misgrounding.
why_possibly_novel: Frame of reference is studied in psycholinguistics and some VQA work; a dense segmentation/detection evaluation of frame control may not exist; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble stimuli with oriented objects (animals, chairs, people) where the two frames disagree; evaluate paired prompts with explicit frame markers; measure frame-following rate.
main_risk: Annotating ground truth for object-centric frames requires care with ambiguous orientations, shrinking usable stimuli.
community_default_belief: Spatial grounding errors are noise; models that handle 'left of' at all are assumed to apply the frame the language specifies.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Caption data almost always uses viewer-centric descriptions, so models plausibly learned a single frame and treat frame markers as noise words.
fastest_falsification: Mirror-flip evaluation: if predictions for 'X's left' fail to flip with the mirrored image in the object-centric way, the bias is confirmed; hours of inference.

one_line: Numerals in dense-prediction prompts do not modulate how many instances get segmented, revealing that count words are treated as noise.
problem: Prompts like 'the three cats' presuppose the model can use cardinality to select or verify instances, but instance count control is never measured.
core_hypothesis: Open-vocabulary and referring segmenters produce statistically indistinguishable instance counts for prompts differing only in the numeral, and their masks do not preferentially cover numeral-consistent subsets.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-instance scenes, the distribution of predicted instance counts will be independent of the prompted numeral, measured by mutual information near zero.
why_important: Cardinality is a basic compositional constraint; if ignored, downstream counting, inventory, and verification applications built on dense VLMs are unsound.
why_possibly_novel: Counting is studied for VQA and generation; numeral-conditioned mask control for dense predictors may be untested; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Scenes with four-plus same-category instances; prompts sweeping numerals; measure dependence between prompted and predicted counts for two public systems.
main_risk: Instance individuation from semantic masks is itself error-prone, adding measurement noise to the count comparison.
community_default_belief: Richer prompts give dense models more constraint to exploit; every content word contributes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive text embeddings are known to blur quantities, and mask decoders have no mechanism to enforce cardinality, so numerals plausibly contribute nothing.
fastest_falsification: Numeral-sweep inference on a few hundred multi-instance images, one day.

one_line: Ordinal references ('second from the left') are resolved by saliency rank, not positional rank, in VLM dense grounding.
problem: Ordinal expressions require ordering objects along an axis and indexing into that order, a computation no dense-grounding architecture explicitly supports.
core_hypothesis: When positional rank and visual saliency rank disagree, dense models select the referent by saliency; error patterns will follow the saliency ordering rather than being uniform.
falsifiable_prediction: On lineup-style scenes with controlled saliency (size, color contrast), the model's chosen referent will match saliency rank significantly more often than positional rank whenever the two conflict.
why_important: Distinguishes 'fails randomly at ordinals' from 'systematically substitutes an easier computation', which informs whether the fix is data or architecture.
why_possibly_novel: Ordinal grounding failures are anecdotal; a saliency-versus-position conflict design for dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate lineup scenes with independently controlled position and saliency; evaluate ordinal prompts; classify errors by which ranking they follow.
main_risk: Saliency is model-dependent, so the conflict design needs a per-model saliency estimate rather than a human one.
community_default_belief: Ordinal failures are part of a general 'counting is hard' story with no finer structure worth modeling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If errors are structured by saliency substitution, they are predictable and exploitable, unlike generic counting noise.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic lineups (rendered shapes) with two public models, inference plus analysis in a day.

one_line: Size comparatives in dense grounding are resolved by pixel area rather than inferred physical size, failing under perspective.
problem: Expressions like 'the larger dog' assume models compare physical magnitudes, but nothing forces the comparison to happen in world units rather than image units.
core_hypothesis: VLM referring systems ground size comparatives by projected pixel area; on scenes where perspective inverts apparent size (the physically larger object is farther and smaller in the image), accuracy on size comparatives will invert accordingly.
falsifiable_prediction: On depth-induced area-inversion scenes, models will select the pixel-larger object in the large majority of trials for 'larger' prompts, performing below chance with respect to physical size.
why_important: Size language is common in disambiguation; a pixel-area heuristic makes models confidently wrong exactly in 3D-rich scenes such as robotics workspaces.
why_possibly_novel: Comparative grounding has been studied in 2D terms; a perspective-inversion stress test tying it to depth reasoning may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or render scenes with two same-category objects where physical and pixel size disagree; evaluate 'larger/smaller' referring prompts and score against physical ground truth.
main_risk: Rendered scenes may leak other cues (texture density, sharpness) that correlate with the intended answer.
community_default_belief: Models integrating depth-aware features implicitly compare physical extents when the language asks for size.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Neither contrastive pretraining nor referring finetuning ever supervises physical-size comparison, so the cheapest consistent heuristic is projected area.
fastest_falsification: A rendered inversion set of a few hundred scenes evaluated on one public model within a day.

one_line: Proximity language ('near the window') contributes almost nothing to dense grounding beyond the landmark noun's co-occurrence prior.
problem: Locative phrases are assumed to guide localization, but the landmark noun alone may explain the behavior via learned object co-occurrence.
core_hypothesis: Ablating the relation word while keeping the landmark ('cup near the window' versus 'cup window') changes predicted masks negligibly, showing that proximity semantics are unused and the landmark acts as a bag-of-words context cue.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask agreement between full locative prompts and relation-ablated prompts will be near the agreement of paraphrase controls, while agreement with landmark-removed prompts drops sharply.
why_important: Clarifies what part of locative expressions dense systems actually consume, which matters for prompt design and for claims about spatial reasoning.
why_possibly_novel: Ablation studies target adjectives and relations broadly; isolating relation-word versus landmark-noun contributions for dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three-condition prompt ablation (full, relation-dropped, landmark-dropped) on a referring benchmark subset with locative expressions, two systems.
main_risk: Ungrammatical ablated prompts may shift text-encoder behavior for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis; paraphrase controls are essential.
community_default_belief: Locative phrases are consumed compositionally, with the relation constraining the spatial search region.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Bag-of-words text towers cannot bind the relation to its arguments, so the only usable signal is which nouns are present.
fastest_falsification: Prompt-ablation inference on existing benchmark expressions containing locatives, hours.

one_line: Per-relation grounding accuracy is predicted by caption-corpus frequency of the relational construction, not by its geometric complexity.
problem: Some spatial relations are grounded better than others, and the variation is usually hand-waved as geometric difficulty.
core_hypothesis: The ordering of relations by dense-grounding accuracy matches their construction frequency in web caption corpora more closely than any geometry-based difficulty measure, implying relation grounding is memorized from language statistics rather than computed.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a set of relations (on, under, beside, inside, behind, between), rank correlation of accuracy with corpus frequency will exceed rank correlation with geometric-complexity ratings from human annotators.
why_important: If relation grounding is frequency-driven, data curation (upsampling rare constructions) is the fix, not architectural spatial modules.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects are shown for object categories; extending the analysis to relational constructions in dense grounding may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-relation accuracy on a referring benchmark, estimate construction frequencies from a public caption corpus, collect geometric-difficulty ratings, and compare correlations.
main_risk: Frequency and geometric simplicity are themselves correlated (common relations tend to be simple), demanding careful partial-correlation analysis.
community_default_belief: Relations like 'between' fail because they are geometrically harder, an inherent difficulty ordering.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Difficulty orderings should transfer across models and data, but if accuracy tracks each model's caption diet, the ordering is contingent, not inherent.
fastest_falsification: Correlation analysis over existing per-relation benchmark breakdowns and corpus counts, no new inference needed if breakdowns exist.

one_line: Negation words in dense-prediction prompts act as positive evidence: 'the man without a hat' increases hat-region activation.
problem: Negated attributes and possessions are common in natural referring expressions, but contrastive text encoders are suspected of encoding negated nouns as if asserted.
core_hypothesis: For VLM dense systems, the negated noun contributes a positive similarity component: masks and attention maps for 'X without Y' overlap the Y-region more than prompts omitting Y entirely, and referent selection fails toward X-with-Y candidates.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired scenes containing both X-with-Y and X-without-Y candidates, prompts negating Y will select the X-with-Y candidate at rates far above chance, and Y-region activation for 'without Y' prompts will exceed that of Y-free prompts.
why_important: Negation failure inverts user intent, which is worse than random error in interactive segmentation and safety-relevant filtering.
why_possibly_novel: Negation blindness is documented for retrieval and generation; a dense-output quantification with paired-candidate scenes may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate scenes with both candidate types; evaluate negated prompts on two referring systems; measure candidate-selection rates and activation on negated-noun regions.
main_risk: Scenes with clean minimal pairs are rare, and synthetic composites may introduce artifacts.
community_default_belief: Negation is a known weak spot but assumed to cause random confusion rather than systematic inversion.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Bag-of-words similarity makes the negated noun add positive score, predicting systematic anti-intent selection, not noise.
fastest_falsification: A small paired-candidate set (even a hundred scenes) evaluated in hours shows whether selection is anti-intent.

one_line: Referring segmentation models almost never abstain: they emit confident masks even when the referent is absent from the image.
problem: Benchmarks guarantee the referent exists, so the absent-referent case, which dominates real usage errors, is untrained and unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Standard referring segmenters produce masks with confidence statistics indistinguishable from present-referent cases when given absent-referent prompts, because no component of the architecture models existence; abstention requires an explicit existence head, not thresholding.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence-based thresholding tuned to any operating point will fail to separate present from absent referents (AUROC near chance), while the same threshold cleanly separates easy from hard present cases.
why_important: Absent-referent hallucination breaks downstream pipelines (editing, robotics) silently; quantifying it changes how systems are deployed and evaluated.
why_possibly_novel: Hallucination is heavily studied for captioning; an existence-calibration analysis for referring segmentation with AUROC-style measurement may be less explored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build absent-referent prompts by shuffling expressions across images with verified absence; measure mask confidence distributions and existence AUROC for two public systems.
main_risk: Verifying true absence requires careful annotation; near-matches (similar categories) can contaminate the negative set.
community_default_belief: Low mask confidence signals absence well enough that thresholding solves the problem in practice.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Confidence in these systems reflects mask-shape certainty, not existence probability; the two are computed by different mechanisms and need not correlate.
fastest_falsification: Expression-shuffling across an existing benchmark gives thousands of absent cases for free; one inference pass suffices.

one_line: Which absent objects a VLM segmenter hallucinates is predictable from the language model's co-occurrence prior alone, before looking at any image.
problem: Dense hallucination is treated as a vision-grounding failure, but LLM-decoder-based segmenters may inherit hallucination structure from text statistics.
core_hypothesis: For LLM-based dense systems, the per-category false-mask rate on images where the category is absent is strongly predicted by the text-only co-occurrence between that category and objects actually present, so hallucination is mostly a language prior leaking through weak visual evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: A regression from text-only co-occurrence scores to per-category false-mask rates will explain a large share of variance, and this share will be higher for LLM-decoder systems than for pure contrastive-matching systems.
why_important: It locates the fix (decoupling language priors from visual evidence) and provides a zero-cost hallucination risk map computable before deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Language-prior-driven hallucination is shown for captioning and VQA; the quantitative transfer of this analysis to dense mask outputs with a cross-architecture comparison may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute text-only co-occurrence priors from the underlying LLM; measure per-category false masks on absence-verified images for one LLM-based and one contrastive system; compare predictive power.
main_risk: Visual confusability (similar-looking categories) correlates with linguistic co-occurrence, requiring visual-similarity controls.
community_default_belief: Dense hallucination reflects visual feature confusion and will fall as vision encoders improve.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the prior comes from the language side, better vision encoders leave the hallucination structure intact whenever visual evidence is ambiguous.
fastest_falsification: Correlate existing hallucination tallies with LLM co-occurrence scores obtained by prompting the text model; analysis-only if tallies exist.

one_line: Open-vocabulary detectors produce more false positives on object-free images than closed-vocabulary counterparts at matched recall, and the gap grows with vocabulary size.
problem: Detection metrics are computed on images dense with annotated objects; behavior on genuinely empty or irrelevant imagery is unreported despite dominating real-world stream data.
core_hypothesis: Querying many text embeddings against every location makes false-positive rate scale with vocabulary size for open-vocabulary detectors, a structural cost of text-query architectures that closed-vocabulary heads do not pay.
falsifiable_prediction: On curated object-free image sets, false positives per image will grow roughly monotonically with query-vocabulary size for open-vocabulary detectors, while closed-vocabulary baselines stay flat, at operating points matched for recall on standard data.
why_important: Streaming applications (surveillance, robotics, moderation) mostly see 'nothing'; a vocabulary-size tax on false alarms changes system design and vocabulary hygiene practices.
why_possibly_novel: Vocabulary-size effects on accuracy are studied; the false-positive scaling law on negative-only data may be uncharacterized; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble verified object-free images (textures, sky, documents); sweep vocabulary sizes for one open-vocabulary detector and one closed baseline; plot false positives versus vocabulary size at matched recall.
main_risk: Truly object-free images are hard to verify at scale, and 'objectness' is partly definitional.
community_default_belief: Open-vocabulary detection matches closed-vocabulary quality while adding flexibility, at no structural cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Each added query is another chance for a spurious match; without a global normalization across queries, the architecture has no mechanism to keep the total false-alarm budget fixed.
fastest_falsification: Vocabulary-size sweep on a few thousand negative images, inference-only, one day.

one_line: Query-order and query-set composition bias per-class dense predictions: the same class scores differently depending on which other classes are queried alongside it.
problem: Open-vocabulary evaluation treats per-class performance as intrinsic, but architectures that softmax or rank across the query set make each class's score depend on its competitors.
core_hypothesis: Per-class IoU/AP shifts materially when the surrounding vocabulary changes (adding distractors, removing rivals), and part of published cross-method differences is actually differences in vocabulary composition handling rather than grounding quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a fixed class within systematically varied query sets will show score swings comparable to typical method-to-method gaps, with predictable direction (rival classes siphon probability mass; unrelated distractors add false positives).
why_important: It undermines the interpretation of per-class numbers and motivates evaluation protocols that marginalize over query-set composition.
why_possibly_novel: Softmax competition is understood in classification; quantifying query-set composition effects as an evaluation confound for dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one segmenter, evaluate ten target classes under nested and shuffled vocabulary contexts; quantify score variance attributable to context versus images.
main_risk: Effects may be architecture-specific (softmax-based versus sigmoid-based scoring), limiting generality of any single result.
community_default_belief: A model's ability to segment 'dog' is a property of the model and the images, independent of what else was asked.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ranking and normalization couple queries by construction; independence was never architecturally true, only assumed.
fastest_falsification: Context-swept re-evaluation of a handful of classes, inference-only, hours to a day.

one_line: Activation maps for pseudo-words (nonsense tokens) predict where dense VLMs will hallucinate real absent objects.
problem: There is no cheap way to identify hallucination-prone image regions before querying; hallucination is discovered only after false masks appear.
core_hypothesis: Querying a VLM dense system with meaningless pseudo-words yields activation concentrated on high-genericity object regions, and these maps overlap strongly with where real absent-category queries produce false masks, revealing a query-independent 'hallucination substrate'.
falsifiable_prediction: Spatial overlap between pseudo-word activation and false-positive masks from real absent-class queries will be far above chance and above overlap with true-positive masks.
why_important: A query-independent hallucination-risk map enables cheap deployment-time gating: suppress or flag matches inside the substrate.
why_possibly_novel: Null-prompt or garbage-prompt probing is used ad hoc for debugging; systematizing it as a predictive hallucination map may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate pseudo-word activation maps for a few hundred images; separately collect false masks from absent-class queries; measure overlap statistics against controls.
main_risk: Pseudo-word embeddings may land near real words in text space, contaminating the 'meaningless query' premise; token-frequency-matched pseudo-words are needed.
community_default_belief: Hallucination is query-specific: a model hallucinates 'dog' where dog-like evidence exists, so no query-free predictor should work.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If false matches are dominated by a generic objectness-plus-saliency component shared across queries, the query mostly selects the label, not the location.
fastest_falsification: One inference pass with a battery of pseudo-words plus reuse of existing false-positive data, a day.

one_line: Negated attributes are dense no-ops: masks for 'the car that is not red' are nearly identical to masks for 'the red car'.
problem: Attribute negation is the simplest compositional operation users apply, and dense systems' handling of it is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: The mask overlap between attribute-affirmed and attribute-negated prompts is close to paraphrase-level overlap, because the attribute word contributes a fixed positive component regardless of negation; systems will preferentially select the attribute-bearing candidate under negation.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes with both a red and a non-red car, 'the car that is not red' will select the red car at rates well above chance, and mean mask IoU between negated and affirmed prompts will approach the paraphrase ceiling.
why_important: Negated attributes appear constantly in interactive correction ('not the red one'); a no-op negation makes correction loops diverge.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute binding is studied; the specific negation-as-no-op quantification at mask level with candidate-selection analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired-candidate scenes with controlled attributes; paired affirmed/negated prompts; measure selection rates and mask overlaps on two systems.
main_risk: Negation phrasing varies ('non-red', 'not red', 'without red paint'); results may be phrasing-sensitive, requiring a phrasing battery.
community_default_belief: Failures on negation are lumped into general compositionality weakness without a specific behavioral signature.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A specific signature (anti-intent selection at paraphrase-level overlap) is stronger and more actionable than 'weak compositionality': it predicts exactly which errors occur.
fastest_falsification: Small paired-candidate benchmark, two prompt phrasings, one model, hours.

one_line: Web-caption frequency of a class name predicts its open-vocabulary dense performance better than annotation count, object size, or visual distinctiveness.
problem: Per-class variation in open-vocabulary segmentation/detection is attributed to visual factors, but the pretraining text distribution is rarely entered as a covariate.
core_hypothesis: A frequency proxy for the class name in web captions is the single strongest predictor of per-class dense performance, dominating visual covariates in a joint regression, implying 'open vocabulary' quality is mostly 'frequent vocabulary' quality.
falsifiable_prediction: In a multivariate regression across many classes and two benchmarks, the caption-frequency term will retain the largest standardized coefficient after controlling for object size, mask count, and intra-class visual variance.
why_important: It reframes open-vocabulary progress: gains may reflect vocabulary coverage of pretraining data, and rare-concept performance claims need frequency-stratified reporting.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects are established for zero-shot classification; a controlled multivariate analysis for dense tasks with visual covariates may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-class dense scores from two benchmarks, estimate name frequencies from a public caption corpus, compute visual covariates, and fit the joint regression.
main_risk: Public corpora are imperfect proxies for proprietary pretraining data, attenuating the measured effect.
community_default_belief: Dense per-class difficulty is primarily visual: small, ambiguous, or deformable objects are hard.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text tower can only retrieve what it has representations for; visual difficulty may be second-order relative to query representation quality.
fastest_falsification: Analysis-only study using published per-class breakdowns plus corpus counts, no new inference.

one_line: Reporting bias in captions creates a grounding gap for visually obvious but rarely mentioned attributes (wetness, material, temperature cues).
problem: Captions mention surprising or identity-relevant properties and omit obvious ones, so VLMs may lack grounding for attributes people never write down despite their visual clarity.
core_hypothesis: Attribute words with high visual detectability but low caption mention rate (because they are pragmatically obvious) will show disproportionately poor dense grounding compared to attributes matched for visual detectability but mentioned often.
falsifiable_prediction: Across an attribute battery with human-rated visual detectability and corpus-estimated mention rates, dense grounding quality will track mention rate strongly after detectability is controlled.
why_important: Identifies a class of blind spots invisible to standard benchmarks (which inherit the same reporting bias) yet critical for robotics and inspection tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Reporting bias is a known concept in vision-language; a dense-grounding quantification with detectability controls may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select attribute pairs matched on human detectability but differing in caption frequency; evaluate dense grounding (segment 'the wet pavement') on curated images; compare within-pair gaps.
main_risk: Human detectability ratings are subjective, and attribute region ground truth is laborious to annotate.
community_default_belief: If a property is visually salient, a large VLM will have learned to ground it from scale alone.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scale amplifies what text supervises; properties systematically omitted from text receive no alignment pressure at any scale.
fastest_falsification: A small matched-pair attribute set with quick manual region annotation, evaluated in a couple of days.

one_line: Web captions are spatially impoverished, so scaling caption data improves noun grounding but not spatial-relation grounding, a divergence measurable on scaling families.
problem: The field expects data scaling to lift all vision-language capabilities, but the caption distribution may contain almost no precise spatial supervision to learn from.
core_hypothesis: Because precise spatial constructions are rare and often wrong in alt-text, relation-grounding performance across a data-scaling family of VLMs will be nearly flat while noun grounding climbs, showing a supervision ceiling rather than a capacity ceiling.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched dense evaluations, the slope of relation-grounding accuracy versus pretraining data size will be a small fraction of the noun-grounding slope for the same checkpoints.
why_important: It predicts that spatial capability requires targeted data or objectives, and that waiting for bigger web scrapes is futile for this axis.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling analyses report aggregate benchmarks; a decomposition into noun versus relation grounding slopes may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a public checkpoint family spanning data scales on paired noun-grounding and relation-grounding dense probes; compare scaling slopes.
main_risk: Available scaling families confound data size with curation changes, muddying slope attribution.
community_default_belief: Emergent capabilities from scale will eventually cover spatial language as they covered object recognition.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Emergence requires the signal to exist in the data; if spatial supervision is absent or noisy at all scales, there is nothing to emerge from.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only evaluation of an existing checkpoint family on two probe sets, days.

one_line: Rare-class dense performance is text-side-bottlenecked: remapping rare names to frequent synonyms recovers most of the gap, capping out at the synonym's own performance.
problem: Poor rare-class performance is usually attacked with visual finetuning, though the failure may sit in the query embedding.
core_hypothesis: For rare classes with a frequent near-synonym, substituting the frequent name recovers a large fraction of the performance gap without touching the vision side, and the recovered performance asymptotes at the frequent synonym's level, identifying the text tower as the binding constraint.
falsifiable_prediction: Synonym remapping will yield gains strongly correlated with the frequency gap between original and substituted names, and residual error after remapping will match the frequent class's error profile.
why_important: A free deployment-time fix, plus a clean method to attribute rare-class failure between text and vision towers.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt rewriting is folk practice; using synonym substitution as a causal attribution instrument with asymptote analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify rare/frequent synonym pairs; evaluate dense performance under both names on the same images; analyze gain versus frequency gap and residual error profiles.
main_risk: True synonyms are rare; near-synonyms shift meaning slightly and can change the correct ground truth region.
community_default_belief: Rare-class failure requires more labeled visual data or few-shot visual adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the vision tower already represents the object and only the query vector is malformed, visual data addresses the wrong tower.
fastest_falsification: Name-substitution inference on existing benchmarks for a dozen synonym pairs, hours.

one_line: Homonym class names are grounded to their caption-dominant sense, and dense systems ignore disambiguating context supplied in the prompt.
problem: Vocabularies contain homonyms (mouse, crane, bat), and it is unknown whether prompt context ('crane, the bird') actually redirects dense predictions.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictions for homonyms follow the corpus-dominant sense regardless of scene content, and appending disambiguating context shifts predictions only marginally because the head noun's embedding dominates the pooled query.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes containing the minority sense, undisambiguated prompts will produce dominant-sense-driven errors, and the disambiguated prompt's improvement will be a small fraction of the gap to an oracle single-sense synonym query.
why_important: Vocabulary designers assume context clauses fix ambiguity; if they do not, deployed vocabularies need sense-specific engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Lexical ambiguity is studied in retrieval; a dense-output sense-dominance analysis with an oracle-synonym yardstick may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect minority-sense scenes for several homonyms; compare bare-name, context-augmented, and oracle-synonym prompts on one segmenter.
main_risk: Some homonyms have visually similar senses, diluting the diagnostic; sense pairs must be visually disjoint.
community_default_belief: Adding clarifying words to the prompt injects the needed semantics, as it does for LLM text tasks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive text pooling can let a frequent head-noun sense dominate the sentence embedding, so appended context is arithmetic noise rather than disambiguation.
fastest_falsification: Three-prompt comparison on a curated minority-sense set, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Proper nouns (brands, landmarks) are dense-grounded disproportionately well relative to matched common nouns, exposing alt-text memorization as a hidden performance component.
problem: Open-vocabulary evaluations mix generic categories with named entities, and the entity performance may reflect memorized image-text co-occurrence rather than compositional grounding.
core_hypothesis: Dense grounding of proper nouns exceeds that of common nouns matched for visual specificity and frequency, because alt-text disproportionately names entities; this gap quantifies how much 'open-vocabulary' skill is retrieval-like memorization.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched pairs (a specific brand's logo versus an equally distinctive generic logo shape; a landmark versus a matched generic building type), proper nouns will show systematically better localization.
why_important: It separates two mechanisms (compositional grounding versus memorized association) that generalize very differently to new concepts.
why_possibly_novel: Entity memorization is discussed for generation and retrieval; a dense-localization matched-pair quantification may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched proper/common pairs with human-verified visual specificity; evaluate localization quality per pair on one open-vocabulary detector.
main_risk: Matching visual specificity across proper and common nouns is subjective and may drive the result if done loosely.
community_default_belief: Open-vocabulary systems generalize compositionally, and entity performance is just another point on the same capability curve.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Alt-text is entity-heavy by economic design (SEO), so entity grounding may be supervised orders of magnitude more densely than generic composition.
fastest_falsification: A few dozen matched pairs evaluated on one model, one day including curation.

one_line: Compound class names activate on their component words: 'fire hydrant' queries produce spurious dense responses on fires and hydrant-unrelated red objects.
problem: Many vocabulary entries are compounds whose meaning is not the sum of parts, but contrastive text encoders may embed them close to their components.
core_hypothesis: Patch-level responses to compound queries decompose approximately linearly into component-word responses, causing predictable false positives on component referents; the decomposition residual (compound minus components) predicts which compounds are safely usable in vocabularies.
falsifiable_prediction: Activation maps for compounds will correlate strongly with the sum of component maps, and false positives will concentrate on component referents (flames for 'fire hydrant', beds of flowers for 'flower pot') at rates far above unrelated-object baselines.
why_important: Vocabulary construction is a deployment-critical, unglamorous step; a compositional-leakage metric would make it principled.
why_possibly_novel: Compositional leakage is studied in text embeddings; a dense-activation decomposition with a usability metric for vocabulary design may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a list of compounds, compute compound and component activation maps on images containing component referents; measure correlation and false-positive concentration.
main_risk: Some component correlation is semantically legitimate (hydrants are near streets), needing careful negative-region definitions.
community_default_belief: Multi-word class names are handled as units by the text encoder; the compound's meaning is what gets matched.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Subword-composed embeddings have no mechanism to suppress component semantics unless pretraining saw the compound often enough to specialize it.
fastest_falsification: Component-map correlation analysis on cached features for a dozen compounds, hours.

one_line: Dense transfer of VLMs degrades sharply beyond the positional-embedding interpolation regime, and the bottleneck is PE handling, not feature quality.
problem: Dense tasks run VLMs far above pretraining resolution, silently relying on positional-embedding interpolation whose failure modes are unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Performance versus inference resolution is smooth within a moderate interpolation range and then deteriorates nonlinearly, and swapping PE-handling strategies (interpolation scheme, windowed attention, PE-free variants) at fixed weights moves the breakdown point, proving the bottleneck is positional, not representational.
falsifiable_prediction: At high resolution multipliers, changing only the PE interpolation scheme will change dense accuracy by more than changing the decoder, and error maps will show characteristic grid-structured artifacts before breakdown.
why_important: Practitioners choose inference resolution by rule of thumb; a characterized breakdown boundary and its dependence on PE strategy would set defaults rationally.
why_possibly_novel: PE interpolation is a known trick; a controlled attribution study of high-resolution dense degradation to PE versus features may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resolution sweep on one frozen VLM with three PE-handling variants and a fixed dense head; localize degradation onset and compare against decoder-variant effects.
main_risk: Attention-pattern shifts at high token counts confound pure PE effects; attention-map diagnostics are needed alongside.
community_default_belief: Higher inference resolution monotonically helps dense tasks, with PE interpolation a solved detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interpolation preserves coarse position but distorts relative-distance geometry that attention heads calibrated at pretraining scale depend on.
fastest_falsification: Resolution-by-PE-scheme grid on one benchmark subset, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Sliding-window inference for VLM dense prediction concentrates errors at window boundaries and systematically loses global-context-dependent classes.
problem: Windowed inference is the default workaround for resolution limits, evaluated only by aggregate metrics that hide spatially structured failure.
core_hypothesis: Error density is elevated in a band around window borders, and classes whose recognition depends on global context (stuff classes, scene-dependent objects) lose disproportionate accuracy under windowing versus full-image inference at matched effective resolution.
falsifiable_prediction: Error heatmaps registered to the window grid will show border bands, and the per-class windowing penalty will correlate with a measured context-dependence score (accuracy drop under context cropping).
why_important: Windowing choices (size, overlap, fusion) are made ad hoc; a characterization of who pays the cost would guide fusion design and flag classes needing global passes.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary artifacts are folklore; quantifying the class-selective global-context loss for VLM dense prediction may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare windowed versus full-image inference on downsampled images (matching effective resolution); compute border-band error statistics and per-class penalties against context-dependence scores.
main_risk: Matching effective resolution between conditions is subtle; mismatches would masquerade as windowing effects.
community_default_belief: With enough overlap, sliding-window inference approximates full-image inference at negligible quality cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Overlap fixes local continuity but cannot restore long-range context that never entered any window.
fastest_falsification: Grid-registered error heatmap on one dataset, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Patch size imposes a hard floor on detectable object size in open-vocabulary detection, unfixable by decoder capacity and predictable by a simple patch-count rule.
problem: Small-object failure in VLM detectors is attributed vaguely to resolution; the specific role of tokenization granularity is not isolated.
core_hypothesis: Recall collapses for objects spanning fewer than a small number of patches regardless of decoder design, because patch pooling destroys sub-patch evidence before any decoder sees it; the collapse point shifts proportionally when patch size changes, at matched compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-size recall curves plotted in units of patches-per-object (rather than pixels) will align across backbones with different patch sizes, exhibiting a shared collapse threshold.
why_important: It converts small-object capability planning into arithmetic (patch size versus target object size), preventing wasted decoder engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object difficulty is well known; the patch-normalized alignment of recall curves as a quantitative invariant may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two backbones differing only in patch size on one detection benchmark; replot per-size recall in patch units and test curve alignment.
main_risk: Backbones differing in patch size usually differ in other respects too; careful matching or patch-size-modified retraining is needed.
community_default_belief: Stronger decoders and feature pyramids can compensate for coarse tokenization on small objects.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Information destroyed at the embedding stage cannot be recreated downstream; pyramids only reshuffle what survived pooling.
fastest_falsification: Patch-unit replotting of existing per-size evaluation results across two models, analysis-only.

one_line: Square-resize pretraining biases VLM dense prediction on extreme aspect ratios, and letterboxing versus stretching is a measurable, class-dependent tradeoff.
problem: Dense inference on panoramas, documents, and vertical video silently reshapes inputs to the pretraining aspect ratio, distorting geometry the dense task depends on.
core_hypothesis: Dense accuracy degrades with aspect-ratio distortion magnitude, and the preferred mitigation differs by class geometry: elongated classes suffer more from stretching while small classes suffer more from letterbox downscaling, making a single preprocessing default wrong.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class dense accuracy under stretch versus letterbox will interact with class elongation and size statistics in the predicted directions, and the crossover will replicate across two backbones.
why_important: Preprocessing is the most-copied, least-examined code in dense pipelines; a characterized tradeoff would change defaults for non-square domains.
why_possibly_novel: Aspect-ratio handling is engineering folklore; a class-geometry-conditioned analysis for VLM dense transfer may be unpublished; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one segmenter on aspect-extreme imagery under stretch, letterbox, and native-ratio tiling; stratify accuracy by class elongation and size.
main_risk: Aspect-extreme datasets with dense labels are scarce, possibly forcing synthetic recomposition with its own artifacts.
community_default_belief: Resize-to-square is a harmless normalization inherited from classification.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Classification needed only invariance; dense tasks need geometry preservation, and the two goals disagree exactly at preprocessing.
fastest_falsification: Three-preprocessing comparison on an existing benchmark's most elongated images, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Token merging and pruning methods benchmarked on VQA silently devastate dense prediction at the same token budgets.
problem: Efficiency methods for VLMs are validated on tasks with global answers, then reused in dense pipelines where per-location information matters.
core_hypothesis: At matched token-reduction ratios, dense metrics degrade several times faster than VQA metrics because merging preferentially destroys within-object boundary tokens that global tasks never needed; the degradation is predictable from merge-map geometry.
