falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping token-reduction ratios will produce a much steeper dense-accuracy decline than VQA decline for the same method and backbone, with errors concentrated where the merge map is coarsest.
why_important: Efficiency claims transfer across tasks in practice; a documented dense-tax would prevent silent quality regressions in deployed dense systems.
why_possibly_novel: Token-merging papers evaluate mostly classification/VQA; a systematic dense-task degradation profile may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply one popular token-merging method at several ratios to a frozen VLM; evaluate both VQA and segmentation; overlay merge maps with error maps.
main_risk: Some merging schemes are content-adaptive and might preserve boundaries better than hypothesized, weakening the general claim.
community_default_belief: Visual tokens are redundant, so aggressive merging is nearly free across tasks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Redundancy is task-relative: tokens redundant for a pooled answer are exactly the ones dense outputs read individually.
fastest_falsification: One merging method, three ratios, two evaluations, one day.

one_line: Multi-crop high-resolution schemes in LLM-based VLMs leave crop-seam inconsistencies detectable as grid-aligned artifacts in dense outputs.
problem: AnyRes-style tiling feeds crops through the encoder independently, and dense heads inherit whatever inconsistency exists across crop borders.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictions from multi-crop VLMs show statistically elevated discontinuity along crop boundaries (label flips, depth jumps) relative to matched within-crop locations, and objects straddling seams suffer measurable accuracy penalties.
falsifiable_prediction: Prediction-discontinuity statistics computed along the crop grid will exceed within-crop baselines, and per-object accuracy will be lower for seam-straddling objects than for size-matched interior objects.
why_important: Multi-crop is becoming the default high-resolution mechanism for VLMs; its dense-task artifacts should be characterized before it is baked into applications.
why_possibly_novel: Crop-tiling is discussed for VQA quality; a dense-artifact characterization along seams may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one multi-crop VLM dense system on standard imagery; compute seam-aligned discontinuity and seam-straddling object penalties versus interior controls.
main_risk: Global-context tokens (thumbnail crop) may partially heal seams, making effects small and model-specific.
community_default_belief: The low-resolution global view plus overlapping crops adequately stitches representations for downstream use.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Stitching is learned only implicitly through language supervision, which never penalizes spatial inconsistency, so nothing enforces seam coherence.
fastest_falsification: Seam-statistics analysis on a few hundred dense outputs, hours after inference.

one_line: VLM features underweight high spatial frequencies, and boundary quality gains more from frequency-targeted feature surgery than from resolution increases at matched cost.
problem: Boundary imprecision in VLM dense prediction is met with higher resolution, which is quadratically expensive and may not address the actual spectral deficit.
core_hypothesis: The frequency spectrum of VLM patch features is biased low relative to dense-supervised backbones, and injecting cheap high-frequency pathways (early-layer skips, edge-aware modulation) improves boundary F-score more per FLOP than resolution scaling.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched additional compute, a high-frequency skip pathway will beat a resolution increase on boundary metrics while roughly tying on interior metrics.
why_important: Boundary quality drives usability in editing and measurement applications; a cheaper lever than resolution changes deployment economics.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency analyses exist for CNNs and ViTs generally; a cost-matched boundary-improvement comparison for VLM dense transfer may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Spectral analysis of features from one VLM versus one dense-supervised backbone; then cost-matched comparison of skip-pathway versus resolution-increase on one benchmark's boundary metrics.
main_risk: Skip pathways add trainable parameters, complicating a clean frozen-feature comparison.
community_default_belief: Boundary softness is a resolution problem: feed more pixels and boundaries sharpen.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the features discard high frequencies regardless of input size, resolution scaling feeds more pixels into the same low-pass filter.
fastest_falsification: Feature spectra comparison is immediate; the cost-matched training comparison fits in a few GPU-days.

one_line: Textual coordinate outputs of VLMs quantize localization: error histograms carry the signature of the coordinate token vocabulary, not visual uncertainty.
problem: LLM-style VLMs emit boxes and points as text, but the tokenization of numbers imposes a discrete lattice whose effect on localization is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Localization residuals cluster at the spacing implied by coordinate token granularity, and total error decomposes into a quantization floor plus a visual term; models with finer coordinate vocabularies show proportionally lower floors independent of visual backbone quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Residual histograms will be multimodal at lattice spacings, and shrinking bin size via re-encoding (normalized coordinates with more tokens) will reduce error on easy, high-contrast targets where visual uncertainty is negligible.
why_important: It separates interface error from perception error, redirecting effort from bigger backbones to better output encodings.
why_possibly_novel: Coordinate-as-text is widely used; a quantization-decomposition analysis of localization error may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one coordinate-emitting VLM on high-contrast synthetic targets; analyze residual histograms; repeat with a finer coordinate encoding via finetuning or prompt-side renormalization.
main_risk: Sampling noise in decoding can blur the lattice signature, requiring greedy decoding and many trials.
community_default_belief: Localization error of VLM detectors reflects visual grounding quality; the text interface is lossless plumbing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A discrete token lattice is definitionally lossy, and its loss lands exactly on the metric dense tasks care about.
fastest_falsification: Residual-histogram analysis of existing predictions against ground truth, analysis-only.

one_line: Autoregressive polygon outputs accumulate error along the vertex sequence, degrading with contour complexity much faster than raster mask formats.
problem: Polygon-as-text is an appealing compact mask format, but autoregressive generation makes later vertices condition on earlier errors.
core_hypothesis: Vertex error grows with sequence position (an error-cascade signature), so polygon formats lose accuracy on high-complexity contours at a rate that raster or query-based mask formats do not; the crossover complexity defines where each format should be used.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-vertex error will increase with position in the generated sequence controlling for local contour curvature, and format comparison stratified by contour complexity will show polygons winning on simple shapes and losing sharply on complex ones.
why_important: Output-format choice is being made by API convenience; a complexity-conditioned characterization would make it evidence-based.
why_possibly_novel: Format comparisons exist at aggregate level; the positional error-cascade analysis within polygon generation may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one polygon-emitting system on shapes stratified by contour complexity; regress vertex error on sequence position with curvature controls; compare against a raster-mask baseline.
main_risk: Vertex correspondence between prediction and ground truth is ambiguous, requiring careful matching methodology.
community_default_belief: Polygon text formats are a compact, accurate mask representation whose errors mirror visual difficulty.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Autoregression adds a sequential error dynamic that has nothing to do with visual difficulty and everything to do with generation order.
fastest_falsification: Position-versus-error regression on existing polygon predictions, analysis-only.

one_line: Decoding hyperparameters (temperature, top-p) change dense grounding metrics of LLM-based VLMs by margins comparable to model-choice differences, yet go unreported.
problem: Dense outputs from generative VLMs are sampled, but papers compare models without controlling or reporting decoding settings.
core_hypothesis: Localization and mask metrics vary substantially across reasonable decoding configurations, sometimes reordering model comparisons, meaning part of reported progress is decoding-configuration luck.
falsifiable_prediction: A decoding-parameter sweep on two public VLM grounding systems will produce metric ranges overlapping across models, and greedy versus sampled decoding will differ systematically (greedy better for coordinates).
why_important: It is a reproducibility hazard: unreported decoding settings make dense-grounding leaderboards partly meaningless.
why_possibly_novel: Decoding sensitivity is known for text quality; its quantification for dense grounding metrics may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep temperature and top-p for two systems on one grounding benchmark; compare within-model metric ranges against between-model gaps.
main_risk: Some systems constrain decoding for coordinate tokens internally, shrinking the effect for those architectures.
community_default_belief: Benchmark differences between VLM grounding systems reflect model quality; decoding is a minor generation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Coordinate tokens are ordinary vocabulary items subject to sampling noise, and a single resampled digit moves a box by many pixels.
fastest_falsification: Decoding sweep on one benchmark subset, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Predicted coordinates from VLMs spike at round numbers, inheriting digit-token priors from language pretraining and biasing localization.
problem: LLMs prefer round numbers in text; if this prior survives grounding finetuning, boxes and points are systematically attracted to round coordinates.
core_hypothesis: Histograms of predicted coordinates show excess mass at round values (multiples of ten, powers of two) beyond what ground-truth distributions justify, and the bias magnitude predicts a recoverable localization error via post-hoc de-biasing.
falsifiable_prediction: Coordinate histograms will show round-value spikes absent from ground truth, spikes will shrink when coordinates are re-encoded in a shifted basis, and simple de-biasing will improve localization on targets near round-value boundaries.
why_important: A free accuracy recovery and a clean demonstration that language priors leak into geometric outputs.
why_possibly_novel: Round-number bias is documented for LLM text; its geometric consequence in dense grounding may be undocumented; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare predicted-versus-ground-truth coordinate histograms for one system; test the shifted-encoding intervention on a finetuned variant or via prompt-side renormalization.
main_risk: Grounding finetuning data may itself contain round-coordinate annotation bias, confounding the source attribution.
community_default_belief: Grounding finetuning overwrites text-statistical priors with visual evidence for numeric outputs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Finetuning reweights but rarely erases pretraining priors, especially for token categories as frequent as digits.
fastest_falsification: Histogram comparison on existing predictions, analysis-only, hours.

one_line: Text-serialized mask formats accumulate error toward the end of the generation order, producing a bottom-right accuracy gradient that flips when the serialization order is reversed.
problem: Serializing masks as token sequences imposes an arbitrary generation order whose spatial consequences are unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Autoregressive drift (context dilution, early-error conditioning) makes later-generated regions less accurate, creating a spatial accuracy gradient aligned with serialization order rather than image content; training with reversed or randomized order relocates the gradient accordingly.
falsifiable_prediction: Error maps averaged over many images will show a gradient aligned with raster order, and a model finetuned with reversed serialization will show the mirrored gradient on the same images.
why_important: Order-dependent accuracy is a hidden artifact that data augmentation cannot fix but order randomization can; diagnosing it changes training recipes for text-mask formats.
why_possibly_novel: Order effects are known in autoregressive image generation; their demonstration in mask-serialization for dense prediction may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or finetune small text-mask models with forward and reversed serialization on identical data; compare spatial error-gradient maps.
main_risk: Content statistics (photographer bias placing subjects centrally) can mimic gradients; the reversal intervention is essential to the design.
community_default_belief: Serialization order is an arbitrary implementation detail with no systematic effect on output quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Every autoregressive system exhibits position-dependent behavior; masks are not exempt merely because the tokens denote pixels.
fastest_falsification: If an order-ablated public model pair exists, error-gradient comparison is analysis-only; otherwise one small paired finetune.

one_line: The textual output format chosen for dense supervision (box corners versus center-size versus polygon) reshapes the model's internal spatial representation, not just its output accuracy.
problem: Format comparisons report endpoint metrics only, leaving unknown whether format choice changes what the model internally knows about space.
core_hypothesis: Models finetuned with different output encodings develop measurably different internal spatial representations (probed for object extent, center, and adjacency), so format is a representational prior: center-size training improves center probing, corner training improves extent probing, beyond what output accuracy differences explain.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes on hidden states of format-matched twins will show a double dissociation aligned with format semantics, persisting even on examples where both models' outputs are correct.
why_important: If format shapes representation, multi-format training becomes a representational tool rather than an output convenience, informing how grounding data should be serialized.
why_possibly_novel: Format comparisons exist at output level; hidden-state dissociation analysis across output encodings may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Finetune one base VLM under two output formats on identical grounding data; probe hidden states for center, extent, and adjacency; test the dissociation.
main_risk: Probing differences can reflect superficial token-context differences rather than genuine spatial knowledge; causal-intervention probes mitigate this.
community_default_belief: Output format is an interface decision; the backbone learns the same spatial understanding regardless.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Gradient flow shapes representations toward the quantities the loss names explicitly, and different formats name different quantities.
fastest_falsification: Paired small-scale finetunes plus probing, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Chain-of-thought prompting improves VLM semantic answers but degrades pointing and dense localization on the same queries.
problem: CoT is promoted as a universal accuracy lever for VLMs, but dense outputs may be harmed by long intermediate token sequences separating perception from emission.
core_hypothesis: Interposed reasoning tokens dilute visual attention available at coordinate-emission time, so CoT trades semantic accuracy for localization accuracy; the localization drop correlates with reasoning-chain length.
falsifiable_prediction: On grounding tasks with and without CoT under matched decoding, localization metrics will decline with CoT while answer-classification components improve or hold, and the decline will grow with generated chain length.
why_important: CoT defaults are being adopted wholesale; knowing it taxes dense outputs changes prompting policy for grounding applications.
why_possibly_novel: CoT evaluations concentrate on QA accuracy; a localization-specific cost analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired CoT/no-CoT evaluation of one VLM on a pointing benchmark, with chain-length stratification and fixed decoding parameters.
main_risk: Prompt phrasing differences between conditions can confound; multiple CoT elicitations are needed.
community_default_belief: More reasoning tokens never hurt: CoT is at worst neutral for any task component.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Attention over a longer context reallocates finite probability mass away from image tokens precisely when coordinates must be read off.
fastest_falsification: Paired-prompt evaluation on one benchmark subset, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Routing all mask information through a single special token (SEG-token architectures) caps multi-instance and fine-detail segmentation by an information bottleneck measurable in instance count.
problem: A popular design has the LLM emit one special token whose hidden state conditions a mask decoder, an architecture whose capacity limits are unquantified.
core_hypothesis: A single token's hidden state cannot encode arbitrarily many instances or high-frequency detail, so accuracy will degrade with required instance count and contour complexity faster than for multi-token or per-query interfaces, and allocating more mask tokens will recover accuracy in proportion.
falsifiable_prediction: Performance versus instance count will fall steeply for single-token interfaces and shallowly for multi-token interfaces at matched backbone, and interpolating token budget will interpolate the curves.
why_important: This architecture is spreading rapidly; its scaling behavior with scene complexity should be known before it ossifies as the default.
why_possibly_novel: Individual papers report aggregate scores; a controlled token-budget versus scene-complexity scaling analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched variants differing only in mask-token budget; evaluate on scenes stratified by instance count and contour complexity.
main_risk: Multi-token variants change optimization dynamics too, so degradation attribution needs care beyond raw capacity.
community_default_belief: The LLM hidden state is rich enough that one conditioning token suffices for segmentation of whatever the language describes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Richness is not addressability: a fixed-width vector summarizing many instances must lose per-instance geometry by counting dimensions.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate an existing single-token system on instance-count-stratified scenes; a steep complexity slope is the cheap first signal, one day.

one_line: VLM-based monocular depth leans on recognized-object size priors and fails systematically on scenes with misleading familiar-size cues (miniatures, forced perspective).
problem: Language-and-recognition-driven depth models may compute 'what objects usually are' rather than geometry, an untested distinction on standard benchmarks where the two coincide.
core_hypothesis: Depth systems built on VLM features weight familiar-size priors heavily, so on miniature scenes, dioramas, and forced-perspective photography their error explodes in the direction the prior predicts, while geometry-first baselines degrade gracefully.
falsifiable_prediction: On a curated misleading-scale test set, VLM-feature depth models will show signed errors consistent with familiar-size assumptions (miniatures rendered too far), and the signed-error pattern will be absent in self-supervised geometric baselines.
why_important: Depth consumers (robotics, AR) encounter atypical-scale scenes routinely; prior-driven confident errors are the dangerous kind.
why_possibly_novel: Familiar-size cues are classical vision knowledge; a targeted stress test attributing modern VLM-depth behavior to them may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble miniature/forced-perspective imagery with approximate ground truth; compare signed error patterns of one VLM-based and one geometry-based depth model.
main_risk: Ground truth for such scenes is hard to obtain; relative-depth ordering within scenes can substitute.
community_default_belief: Better semantic understanding straightforwardly improves depth: knowing what things are helps know where they are.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Semantics helps only when the world matches its statistics; it becomes an adversary exactly when scale expectations break.
fastest_falsification: Signed-error analysis on a small curated set with ordinal ground truth, days including curation.

one_line: Text conditioning in language-conditioned depth and dense-geometry models is largely a no-op: ablating or shuffling the prompt barely changes outputs.
problem: Several systems advertise language-conditioned dense geometry, but whether the language pathway carries causal weight is unverified.
core_hypothesis: Because geometric supervision dominates training gradients, the text branch atrophies: prompt ablation, shuffling, or contradiction changes dense outputs by less than internal sampling noise, so the 'language-conditioned' label describes the architecture, not the function.
falsifiable_prediction: Output change under prompt randomization will be statistically indistinguishable from run-to-run variance for most inputs, and any prompt-sensitive minority of pixels will concentrate on semantically ambiguous regions.
why_important: If the language pathway is dead, claimed controllability is illusory and compute spent on text towers in these systems is waste.
why_possibly_novel: Pathway-atrophy analyses exist for multimodal fusion generally; applying causal prompt-ablation methodology to dense geometry systems may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one language-conditioned depth system, compare output deltas under prompt ablation/shuffle/contradiction against stochastic baseline deltas, pixel-stratified.
main_risk: Some systems may use language only in rare ambiguous cases by design, making a global no-op conclusion unfair without stratification.
community_default_belief: If a text encoder is wired in and the paper shows a prompt-conditioned example, language meaningfully steers the dense output.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Cherry-picked steering examples survive even when the pathway is causally negligible on the input distribution at large.
fastest_falsification: Prompt-randomization deltas on a few hundred images, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Depth decoded from VLM features is piecewise-constant per object: good at per-object median depth, poor at within-object depth gradients.
problem: Aggregate depth metrics hide the decomposition between placing objects at the right distance and reconstructing surface geometry within objects.
core_hypothesis: Semantic features support object-level depth assignment but lack surface-gradient information, so VLM-feature depth error decomposes into small between-object and large within-object components, the reverse of geometry-pretrained features.
falsifiable_prediction: An error decomposition using instance masks will show VLM-feature models with a higher within-object-to-between-object error ratio than self-supervised geometric models at matched overall score.
why_important: Applications differ in which component matters (navigation needs between-object, grasping needs within-object); the decomposition should drive backbone choice.
why_possibly_novel: Depth error decompositions exist; contrasting VLM-semantic versus geometric features through this lens may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two depth models (VLM-feature and geometric) on a benchmark with instance masks; decompose errors into per-object median and within-object residual components.
main_risk: Matching overall score between models to make ratios comparable may require careful checkpoint selection.
community_default_belief: Depth quality is one number; a better mIoU-style depth score means better geometry across the board.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Two models with equal aggregate error can have opposite error anatomies, and semantic features plausibly buy exactly one anatomy.
fastest_falsification: Decomposition analysis on existing predictions with instance masks, analysis-only.

one_line: VLM-derived depth relies on the vertical-position-in-image shortcut and breaks under camera roll and unusual viewpoints far more than geometric baselines.
problem: Ground-plane scenes make image height a strong depth cue; models may exploit it as a shortcut that fails off-distribution.
core_hypothesis: Because caption-style pretraining and depth finetuning share upright-camera statistics, VLM-feature depth weights the y-coordinate cue heavily; rotating inputs degrades it disproportionately, and attribution analysis will show y-position dominance.
falsifiable_prediction: Under controlled input rotation, depth error of VLM-feature models will grow faster with roll angle than that of geometry-pretrained models, and simple attribution will show elevated dependence on vertical position at zero roll.
why_important: Drones, headsets, and manipulators see rolled and tilted views constantly; a hidden upright assumption is a deployment hazard.
why_possibly_novel: The height cue is classical; a comparative shortcut-reliance quantification for modern VLM-based depth may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rotation-sweep evaluation of two depth systems on the same scenes, plus positional-attribution analysis at canonical orientation.
main_risk: Rotation also breaks other cues (sky position), so attribution needs multiple diagnostics rather than roll alone.
community_default_belief: Modern depth models learn viewpoint-robust geometry, having seen diverse imagery at scale.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Web imagery is overwhelmingly upright, so scale reinforces rather than removes the upright prior.
fastest_falsification: Roll-sweep inference on one benchmark, hours.

one_line: Scene-description prompts causally shift the metric scale of language-aware depth models, revealing exploitable and dangerous language-prior leakage.
problem: If language can shift depth scale, then wrong or adversarial descriptions corrupt geometry, but this causal pathway is untested.
core_hypothesis: Prompting a language-aware depth system with contradictory scene types ('a photo of a vast canyon' for an indoor scene) shifts predicted metric scale in the prior-consistent direction, showing that scale is partly read off language rather than pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: A prompt-contradiction battery will produce systematic, direction-predictable scale shifts significantly larger than paraphrase-control shifts.
why_important: It simultaneously demonstrates a safety hazard (caption injection changes geometry) and an opportunity (deliberate scale hints for ambiguous scenes).
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-injection studies target semantic outputs; a metric-scale causal analysis for dense geometry may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one language-aware depth model, evaluate matched images under true, contradictory, and paraphrase prompts; measure scale-factor distributions per condition.
main_risk: If idea B-054's no-op finding holds for the tested system, this experiment needs a system with a genuinely live language pathway; the two studies are natural complements.
community_default_belief: Depth scale comes from visual cues and camera geometry; text inputs are auxiliary context that cannot override pixels.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Monocular metric scale is fundamentally underdetermined by pixels, so any learnable prior, including a linguistic one, will be recruited to resolve it.
fastest_falsification: Three-condition prompt battery on one model, inference-only, hours.

one_line: VLM-feature depth quality drops on unrecognized objects even when their geometry is trivially simple, demonstrating category-mediated rather than geometric depth computation.
problem: If depth is computed through recognition, novel objects get bad geometry regardless of shape simplicity, an inversion of how geometry should work.
core_hypothesis: Per-object depth error of VLM-feature models correlates with recognition confidence rather than shape complexity: simple unfamiliar shapes (blank boxes, abstract forms) receive worse depth than complex familiar objects at matched size and placement.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled scenes containing familiar and unfamiliar objects of matched simplicity and position, the unfamiliar objects will show elevated depth error for VLM-feature models but not for geometric baselines.
why_important: Warehouses, labs, and construction sites are full of unfamiliar shapes; category-mediated depth silently fails exactly there.
why_possibly_novel: Recognition-depth entanglement is hypothesized informally; a matched-complexity familiar/unfamiliar controlled test may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose or photograph scenes with matched familiar/unfamiliar object pairs; evaluate per-object depth error for one VLM-based and one geometric model.
main_risk: Unfamiliar objects may also have unusual textures, confounding recognition with low-level cue differences.
community_default_belief: Depth is a low-level capability that transfers to any object once a model is trained broadly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Nothing forces a depth head on semantic features to learn low-level geometry when category priors explain the training data more cheaply.
fastest_falsification: A small controlled scene set (even rendered) with paired objects, evaluated in days.

one_line: Spatial-QA competence and dense-geometry competence dissociate across VLM systems: models answer 'which is closer' correctly while their dense depth is wrong, and vice versa.
problem: Spatial-QA benchmarks are increasingly used as evidence of 3D understanding, implicitly standing in for dense geometric capability.
core_hypothesis: QA and dense geometry draw on partially disjoint mechanisms (verbal priors and object statistics versus per-pixel evidence), so across a model population the two scores correlate weakly, and per-image agreement between the QA answer and the model's own dense output is far from perfect, exposing internal inconsistency.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-model correlation between spatial-QA accuracy and dense depth quality will be weak, and within single models, QA answers will contradict the model's own dense predictions on a substantial fraction of images.
why_important: Benchmark policy: if QA does not certify dense geometry, claims about 'spatial understanding' need task-matched evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Both task families are evaluated separately; the internal-consistency analysis (model versus its own dense output) may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several systems exposing both interfaces, evaluate paired QA and dense depth on shared images; compute cross-model correlation and within-model contradiction rates.
main_risk: Few systems expose both interfaces cleanly, limiting the model population and statistical power.
community_default_belief: Spatial-QA benchmarks are a convenient, valid proxy for a model's geometric understanding.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Multiple-choice spatial questions are answerable from priors and coarse cues that never touch the dense representation being credited.
fastest_falsification: Contradiction-rate measurement on one dual-interface system, one day.

one_line: Metric-scale accuracy of VLM-era depth models depends on incidental scale metadata correlations (scene type, camera signature) and collapses to relative depth when those cues are randomized.
problem: Metric depth from a single image requires an absolute scale source, and where modern models actually get it from is poorly characterized.
core_hypothesis: Models infer scale from dataset-correlated cues (indoor/outdoor type, lens rendering, typical object sets) rather than from geometry; on images where such cues are neutralized or set into conflict, metric error inflates dramatically while relative (ordinal) accuracy is preserved.
falsifiable_prediction: A cue-conflict test set (indoor-styled outdoor scenes, unusual focal-length renderings) will show large metric-scale errors with preserved depth ordering, and error direction will follow the misleading cue.
why_important: Users treat metric outputs as measurements; knowing they are prior-driven estimates with brittle scale changes how downstream systems consume them.
why_possibly_novel: The scale-source question is acknowledged qualitatively; a cue-conflict decomposition separating metric from ordinal degradation may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a cue-conflict set via curation and rendering; evaluate metric and ordinal metrics separately for two metric-depth systems.
main_risk: Constructing convincing cue-conflict imagery without introducing rendering artifacts is nontrivial.
community_default_belief: Metric depth models have learned genuine scale estimation that generalizes across scene types.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Absolute scale is unobservable in a single image without size priors; the only question is which priors, and dataset-correlated shortcuts are the cheapest to learn.
fastest_falsification: Ordinal-versus-metric metric split on any out-of-distribution scene set, analysis of existing predictions first, days for the full conflict set.

one_line: Base/novel splits in open-vocabulary benchmarks leak through web pretraining: 'novel' classes are often pretraining-frequent, so benchmarks measure vocabulary recall, not generalization.
problem: Open-vocabulary evaluation assumes held-out classes are genuinely unseen, but web-scale pretraining saw text and images of most 'novel' classes abundantly.
core_hypothesis: Performance on 'novel' classes is strongly stratified by their pretraining-frequency proxy, and the subset of genuinely rare novel classes shows a dramatically larger base-novel gap, meaning headline open-vocabulary gains concentrate on pseudo-novel classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Splitting novel classes into frequency terciles will reveal a steep performance gradient, with the rare tercile showing a much larger gap to base classes than the aggregate numbers suggest.
why_important: It recalibrates what open-vocabulary progress means and motivates frequency-stratified reporting as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination concerns are voiced informally; a frequency-stratified re-analysis of standard base/novel dense benchmarks may be unpublished; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute frequency proxies for novel classes of one detection and one segmentation benchmark; re-report published or reproduced per-class results by tercile.
main_risk: Frequency proxies from public corpora imperfectly track proprietary pretraining sets, blurring strata.
community_default_belief: Base/novel protocol isolates generalization to unseen categories, which is what reported gains demonstrate.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Unseen-by-the-detector-head is not unseen-by-the-backbone, and the backbone is where open-vocabulary ability lives.
fastest_falsification: Tercile re-analysis of published per-class breakdowns where available, analysis-only.

one_line: String-matched class scoring in open-vocabulary evaluation penalizes correct predictions under alternative names, and the automatic-versus-human evaluation gap grows with vocabulary openness.
problem: Open-vocabulary systems can output reasonable synonyms or hypernyms for a region, but evaluation counts anything but the canonical string as wrong.
core_hypothesis: A human-judged or embedding-similarity-judged re-scoring of open-vocabulary dense predictions will recover substantial performance relative to exact-match scoring, and the recovery will differ across methods, changing some rankings, because methods differ in name-choice behavior rather than grounding quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-scoring the same predictions with meaning-aware matching will change absolute scores substantially and swap at least some adjacent leaderboard positions.
why_important: If rankings partly reflect name-matching luck, method development is being steered by an artifact.
why_possibly_novel: Meaning-aware scoring exists in captioning; its systematic application to dense open-vocabulary leaderboards may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect predictions from three systems on one benchmark; re-score with human judgment on a sample and an embedding-based matcher at scale; compare rankings under both scorings.
main_risk: Meaning-aware matchers have their own biases, requiring a human-judged anchor sample for calibration.
community_default_belief: Exact class-string matching is an acceptable approximation since vocabularies are fixed at evaluation time.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The premise of open vocabulary is that many names fit a region; freezing one canonical name per region contradicts the capability being measured.
fastest_falsification: Human re-judgment of a few hundred 'errors' from one system reveals the misscoring rate in a day.

one_line: Decomposing referring-segmentation error into grounding (wrong object) versus delineation (right object, bad mask) reorders model rankings and reveals divergent failure profiles.
problem: Referring segmentation reports single IoU numbers that conflate choosing the wrong object with imprecisely masking the right one, two failures with entirely different fixes.
core_hypothesis: Models differ qualitatively in their grounding-versus-delineation error mix at similar aggregate IoU, so component-wise evaluation changes rankings and shows that some celebrated architectures win only one component.
falsifiable_prediction: Component-decomposed evaluation of several public systems will show ranking disagreements between components, and aggregate-IoU-matched model pairs will exhibit significantly different grounding error rates.
why_important: Component-blind metrics steer research toward whichever component is cheapest to improve, not the one that matters for a use case.
why_possibly_novel: Error decompositions exist for detection; a standardized grounding/delineation decomposition for referring segmentation with cross-model re-ranking may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define an instance-matching rule to classify each prediction as grounding-correct or not; re-evaluate three systems component-wise on one benchmark.
main_risk: The decomposition depends on instance annotations and a matching threshold whose choice must be shown not to drive conclusions.
community_default_belief: Overall IoU is an adequate summary of referring-segmentation quality for comparing methods.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A metric blind to the distinction between 'wrong object, perfect mask' and 'right object, sloppy mask' cannot inform either the referring or the segmentation research agenda.
fastest_falsification: Component re-scoring of existing predictions on a benchmark with instance masks, analysis-only.

one_line: Web-pretrained VLM dense results are inflated by test-image overlap with pretraining crawls, and the inflation is measurable via near-duplicate stratification.
problem: Benchmark images circulate on the web and enter pretraining crawls, but dense-task evaluations almost never report contamination analysis.
core_hypothesis: Dense performance on test images with detectable near-duplicates in accessible crawl indices is systematically higher than on verified-clean images, and the gap is larger for open-vocabulary methods than for closed-vocabulary supervised baselines, quantifying contamination-driven inflation.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying one benchmark by near-duplicate presence in a public crawl index will show a significant performance gap in the predicted direction, larger for web-pretrained systems.
why_important: Contamination-corrected numbers may shrink claimed zero-shot gaps, changing the narrative about how much dense ability emerges from web pretraining.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination studies cover LLMs and classification; dense-task contamination stratification may be rare or absent; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run near-duplicate detection between one benchmark's test set and a public crawl corpus; compare dense metrics across duplicate/clean strata for two systems.
main_risk: Near-duplicate detection has false negatives, and clean strata may differ in content difficulty, requiring difficulty controls.
community_default_belief: Dense benchmarks are effectively uncontaminated because pixel-level labels are not on the web, so pretraining exposure does not matter.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Seeing the image (even unlabeled) can teach instance-specific features that transfer to test time; labels are not the only leakage channel.
fastest_falsification: Duplicate detection plus stratified re-scoring on one benchmark, days.

one_line: Cross-paper comparisons of open-vocabulary segmentation are dominated by inconsistent background/ignore-label conventions rather than method differences.
problem: Benchmarks and codebases differ silently in how unlabeled regions, ignore labels, and the background class enter the metric, and papers inherit whichever convention their starting codebase used.
core_hypothesis: Re-evaluating several published methods under one unified convention will compress or reorder reported differences, showing that convention variance is comparable to claimed method improvements in this literature.
falsifiable_prediction: The spread of scores for a single method across conventions will be comparable to the median cross-method gap reported in recent papers.
why_important: If conventions swamp methods, the literature's incremental-improvement signal is unreliable and a standardization effort has higher value than another method.
why_possibly_novel: Convention pitfalls are known to insiders; a quantified convention-variance audit for open-vocabulary segmentation may be unpublished; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take three public checkpoints; evaluate each under three documented conventions (background scored, ignored, thresholded); tabulate convention-induced spread against published method gaps.
main_risk: Reproducing published pipelines faithfully enough to isolate convention effects takes engineering care.
community_default_belief: Reported numbers on the same benchmark name are comparable across papers.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The benchmark name underdetermines the metric; the convention is part of the metric and it varies silently.
fastest_falsification: One checkpoint scored under three conventions, a day, immediately shows the spread magnitude.

one_line: Per-benchmark prompt curation is unacknowledged test-set tuning: standardized frozen prompt protocols would materially reorder open-vocabulary dense leaderboards.
problem: Methods ship hand-tuned prompt templates and class-name lists per benchmark, tuned by evaluating on that benchmark, which is hyperparameter fitting on test data.
core_hypothesis: A frozen, shared prompt protocol (fixed templates, fixed names, no per-benchmark curation) will change method rankings, and the methods that drop most will be those whose ablations attribute the least gain to architecture.
falsifiable_prediction: Under the frozen protocol, at least some published ranking gaps will invert, and the correlation between prompt-curation intensity (as documentable from released code) and score drop will be positive.
why_important: It cleans a systematic optimistic bias from the literature and establishes a fairer comparison standard.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-tuning-as-leakage is discussed for classification; an enforcement-and-reranking study for dense benchmarks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate three or four public dense systems under one frozen prompt protocol; compare rankings against published ones and against code-documented curation intensity.
main_risk: Some methods legitimately co-designed prompts with architecture, so separating fair adaptation from leakage requires judgment calls.
community_default_belief: Prompt engineering is a legitimate part of each method, so evaluating each method with its own prompts is fair.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When the prompts were selected by observing test performance, they encode test-set information no matter how legitimate the engineering feels.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-protocol re-evaluation of two systems on one benchmark, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Adding verified-absent 'negative vocabulary' queries to open-vocabulary dense evaluation reorders models by exposing hallucination costs that standard AP never charges.
problem: Standard evaluation only queries classes present in the annotation set, so confident false masks for absent classes cost nothing.
core_hypothesis: Models differ widely in absent-query false-positive behavior at matched present-query accuracy, so a combined metric charging for negative-query responses will separate models that current benchmarks call equivalent and demote some leaders.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating several systems with an added negative-query battery will reveal at least one leaderboard inversion relative to standard AP, and the negative-query false-positive rate will be poorly predicted by standard AP.
why_important: Deployed systems face mostly absent queries; an evaluation blind to that regime certifies the wrong models.
why_possibly_novel: Negative-aware evaluation exists in niches; a systematic negative-vocabulary protocol for open-vocabulary dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct absence-verified query sets for one benchmark; evaluate three systems on present and absent queries; compare joint-metric rankings with standard rankings.
main_risk: Verifying absence exhaustively is labor-intensive; sampling-based verification with confidence bounds is the practical path.
community_default_belief: High AP on present classes implies a well-calibrated system whose false-alarm behavior is acceptable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: AP conditions on presence by construction; it contains literally zero information about the absent-query regime.
fastest_falsification: Negative-query battery on two systems using categories absent by dataset design, one day.

one_line: Reported small-object gains in VLM dense prediction are within annotation noise: human inter-annotator disagreement at small scales exceeds typical method-to-method differences.
problem: Leaderboard progress on small-object segmentation/detection assumes ground truth is reliable at scales where annotators can barely see or delineate objects.
core_hypothesis: At the smallest object-size strata, inter-annotator IoU/agreement is low enough that the plausible ground-truth noise band contains most published method gaps, so claimed small-object improvements are not statistically interpretable without noise-corrected metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: A multi-annotator relabeling of small objects from one benchmark will show inter-annotator disagreement exceeding the median published method gap in the same size stratum.
why_important: Redirects small-object research toward noise-aware evaluation and better annotation before more modeling.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation noise is studied at dataset level; a size-stratified noise-versus-method-gap comparison for dense VLM claims may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have several annotators independently relabel a sample of small objects; compute agreement statistics; compare against published method gaps in matched strata.
main_risk: Annotator quality varies; the study needs enough annotators and quality control to bound noise credibly.
community_default_belief: Ground truth is ground truth; a higher small-object AP means a better model.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When the referee cannot see the play, the score is a coin flip; metrics inherit the annotators' perceptual limits.
fastest_falsification: Relabel a few hundred small instances with three annotators; agreement statistics take days including annotation.

one_line: Per-pixel confidence from VLM segmenters is miscalibrated in a class- and region-structured way that no single temperature can fix.
problem: Calibration for open-vocabulary segmentation is either ignored or handled with one global temperature borrowed from classification practice.
core_hypothesis: Calibration error varies systematically with class frequency, region type (boundary versus interior), and query-set composition, so global temperature scaling leaves large conditional miscalibration; a structured calibrator (per-frequency-tier, distance-to-boundary-aware) removes most of it.
falsifiable_prediction: Reliability analysis stratified by class tier and boundary distance will show opposite-signed miscalibration across strata (over-confident on rare classes and boundaries, under-confident elsewhere), which global temperature provably cannot fix simultaneously.
why_important: Downstream consumers threshold these confidences; structured miscalibration turns thresholds into class- and geometry-dependent traps.
why_possibly_novel: Segmentation calibration is studied for closed-set models; a structured decomposition for open-vocabulary VLM segmenters may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute stratified reliability diagrams for one VLM segmenter on one benchmark; fit global versus structured calibrators; compare conditional calibration error.
main_risk: Stratified calibration estimates need many pixels per stratum; rare-class strata may be underpowered.
community_default_belief: Temperature scaling, the classification workhorse, adequately calibrates dense predictions too.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dense predictions mix heterogeneous sub-populations (boundaries, interiors, rare queries) whose miscalibrations differ in sign, which a scalar cannot correct.
fastest_falsification: Stratified reliability diagrams from cached predictions, analysis-only, hours.

one_line: Spatial autocorrelation of dense-prediction errors breaks the effective-sample-size assumptions of conformal and risk-control methods applied per pixel.
problem: Distribution-free uncertainty methods are being ported to segmentation by treating pixels as exchangeable units, though errors arrive in large correlated blobs.
core_hypothesis: The spatial correlation length of VLM segmentation errors is large enough that nominal per-pixel guarantees are badly miscovered at the image and region level; correcting with measured effective sample sizes restores advertised coverage at the cost of wider sets.
falsifiable_prediction: Empirical coverage of naive per-pixel conformal sets will fall short of nominal levels on image-level and object-level events, and the shortfall will be predicted by measured error-correlation length.
why_important: Safety cases increasingly cite conformal guarantees; guarantees that quietly assume pixel independence are pseudo-guarantees.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal segmentation papers exist; an autocorrelation-aware audit quantifying the miscoverage and its predictor may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate naive pixel-level conformal masks for one segmenter; measure object-level empirical coverage; correlate shortfall with per-image error correlation length.
main_risk: Defining the practically relevant coverage event (pixel, object, image) involves choices that affect the headline conclusion.
community_default_belief: Conformal methods are assumption-light, so applying them per pixel yields valid uncertainty for segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Exchangeability across pixels within an image is precisely the assumption dense errors violate most flagrantly.
fastest_falsification: Coverage audit on existing predictions with one calibration split, analysis-only, a day.

one_line: Variance across prompt paraphrases is a stronger per-pixel error predictor for VLM dense prediction than standard confidence or MC dropout.
problem: Dense uncertainty estimation reuses vision-only tools (dropout, ensembles) and ignores the text input as a cheap source of controlled perturbation.
core_hypothesis: Because dense errors are often driven by query-embedding fragility, the pixel-wise variance of predictions across meaning-preserving paraphrases identifies error-prone regions better than logit confidence or dropout variance, at a handful of extra inference passes.
falsifiable_prediction: On error-prediction metrics (AUROC of predicting per-pixel mistakes), paraphrase-variance will beat logit confidence and dropout variance for open-vocabulary segmenters, with the advantage concentrated on text-sensitive classes.
why_important: A practical, architecture-agnostic uncertainty signal that directly exploits the multimodal structure everyone else ignores.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ensembling for accuracy is common; using paraphrase variance as a per-pixel uncertainty estimator with head-to-head comparison may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate paraphrase sets for one benchmark's classes; compute the three uncertainty signals for one model; compare error-prediction AUROC pixel-wise.
main_risk: Paraphrase quality control matters: meaning-shifting paraphrases inflate variance for the wrong reason.
community_default_belief: Uncertainty lives in the vision pathway; text input is a fixed conditioning variable, not a perturbation axis.
why_that_may_be_wrong: In open-vocabulary systems the text embedding is half the computation; ignoring its sensitivity discards half the uncertainty.
fastest_falsification: Paraphrase battery of a handful of variants per class on a benchmark subset, inference plus analysis in a day.

one_line: Most calibration error in VLM segmentation is boundary-localized, so global calibration metrics mislead and distance-conditioned calibration is the right primitive.
problem: Papers report a single expected-calibration-error number for segmentation, implicitly averaging two regimes (boundary and interior) with different physics.
core_hypothesis: Decomposing calibration by distance to the nearest ground-truth boundary will show the bulk of miscalibration mass within a thin boundary band; models ranked by global calibration reorder under interior-only calibration, and a distance-conditioned temperature fixes most of the total error.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary-band pixels will exhibit several-fold higher calibration error than interior pixels, and interior-only rankings of models will differ from global rankings.
why_important: Consumers who only need interior reliability (area estimation) or only boundary reliability (measurement) are currently served by one misleading number.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary uncertainty is intuited; the calibration-mass decomposition and re-ranking consequence for VLM segmenters may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute distance-stratified calibration for three segmenters on one benchmark; fit distance-conditioned temperatures; compare residual error against global temperature.
main_risk: Annotation boundary noise itself concentrates in the same band, entangling model miscalibration with label uncertainty.
community_default_belief: A single ECE number meaningfully characterizes a segmentation model's calibration.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Averaging regimes with opposite reliability profiles produces a number describing neither, like averaging day and night temperatures.
fastest_falsification: Distance-stratified reliability analysis from cached predictions, hours.

one_line: Abstention thresholds for open-vocabulary dense prediction do not transfer across query vocabularies, making per-vocabulary recalibration a hidden deployment requirement.
problem: Practitioners tune a rejection threshold once and reuse it as the vocabulary evolves, assuming score scales are vocabulary-stable.
core_hypothesis: Similarity-score distributions shift with vocabulary size and composition (via normalization and competition effects), so a threshold tuned on one vocabulary yields wildly different precision-recall operating points on another; the shift is predictable from vocabulary statistics, enabling analytic threshold correction.
falsifiable_prediction: A threshold-transfer matrix across vocabularies will show large operating-point drift correlated with vocabulary size and inter-class text similarity, and an analytic correction using those statistics will recover most of the intended operating point.
why_important: Silent operating-point drift is a production incident generator; an analytic correction is a cheap fix nobody currently ships.
why_possibly_novel: Score-distribution shift is known in retrieval; a threshold-transfer characterization with analytic correction for dense prediction may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one segmenter, tune thresholds on several vocabularies; evaluate all thresholds on all vocabularies; regress drift on vocabulary statistics and test the correction.
main_risk: Architectures differ in scoring normalization, so the correction may need per-family forms.
community_default_belief: A confidence threshold is a model property that persists across reasonable vocabulary changes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The score is a competition outcome among queries, so changing the competitors changes the score scale by construction.
fastest_falsification: Threshold-transfer matrix over three vocabularies, inference-only, a day.

one_line: In LLM-based segmenters, verbalized uncertainty and mask confidence are uncorrelated: the model 'says' it is unsure while emitting high-confidence masks, and vice versa.
problem: Systems that both talk and segment have two uncertainty channels, and consumers implicitly assume they agree.
core_hypothesis: Verbalized confidence (elicited via standard prompts) and mask-head confidence are computed by weakly coupled mechanisms, so their correlation across examples is low and neither dominates as an error predictor; their disagreement itself is an informative error flag.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a benchmark, the correlation between the two channels will be weak, and a disagreement-based flag will predict errors better than either channel alone.
why_important: Interactive systems surface verbalized confidence to users while pipelines consume mask confidence; unnoticed divergence misleads one audience or the other.
why_possibly_novel: Verbalized-calibration studies target QA; the dual-channel consistency analysis for dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one talk-and-segment system, elicit verbalized confidence and record mask confidence per example; measure correlation and the disagreement flag's error-prediction power.
main_risk: Verbalized confidence elicitation is prompt-sensitive, requiring multiple elicitation formats to bound the effect.
community_default_belief: A model's stated uncertainty reflects its internal uncertainty, including about its dense outputs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Verbalization is generated by the language head from text-level features, while mask confidence comes from a separate decoder; nothing in training aligns them.
fastest_falsification: Dual-channel logging on a benchmark subset, one inference pass plus analysis.

one_line: Distance of a query embedding from the pretraining caption manifold predicts per-query dense reliability, giving a deployment-time reliability score with no labels.
problem: There is no accepted way to predict, before seeing outcomes, whether an open-vocabulary system will be reliable for a particular query string.
core_hypothesis: Queries embedding far from the density of pretraining-like caption embeddings (approximated by a public caption corpus) receive systematically worse dense performance, and this text-side distance is a stronger reliability predictor than query length, frequency, or visual difficulty proxies.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many queries, rank correlation between manifold distance and per-query dense performance will be strong and will survive controls for frequency and length.
why_important: A pre-deployment query linter ('this vocabulary entry is unreliable') would prevent entire categories of production failure at negligible cost.
why_possibly_novel: Out-of-distribution scoring in text space exists for NLP; using caption-manifold distance as a dense-reliability predictor may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a density model on caption embeddings from a public corpus; score benchmark class names; correlate with per-class dense metrics for two systems, with frequency and length controls.
main_risk: Public caption corpora may mismatch the model's actual pretraining distribution, attenuating the signal.
community_default_belief: Reliability must be estimated empirically per class from labeled data; there is no free predictor.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text tower's training density is the mechanism behind per-class variation, so measuring it directly should predict the variation it causes.
fastest_falsification: Density scoring plus correlation with published per-class numbers, analysis-only, a day.

one_line: Dense finetuning collapses open-vocabulary alignment early and abruptly rather than gradually, and the collapse is detectable within the first fraction of training.
problem: Finetuning VLMs for segmentation is known to hurt open-vocabulary breadth, but the dynamics (when, how fast, which classes first) are uncharacterized, so mitigations are applied blindly.
core_hypothesis: Vocabulary breadth (zero-shot performance on held-out class sets) drops in a sharp early phase tied to large initial gradient norms, not smoothly over training, so cheap interventions targeted at the first phase (warmup, text-tower freezing, gradient clipping) preserve most breadth at no dense-accuracy cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking held-out vocabulary metrics per training step will show most breadth loss within an early fraction of steps, and early-phase-only interventions will retain most breadth while matching final dense accuracy.
why_important: Turns 'finetuning forgets' folklore into a characterized dynamic with a targeted, low-cost fix.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting curves exist for classification continual learning; step-resolved breadth-collapse analysis for dense VLM finetuning may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Finetune one VLM for segmentation while evaluating held-out vocabulary breadth at dense checkpoint intervals; test early-phase interventions against full-course ones.
main_risk: Breadth metrics are noisy at high checkpoint frequency; efficient proxy evaluations are needed.
community_default_belief: Forgetting accumulates gradually with training steps, so mitigation must span the whole run (joint training, replay).
why_that_may_be_wrong: The largest representation displacement happens when gradients first hit a mismatched head; after re-equilibration, drift may be minor.
fastest_falsification: One finetuning run with dense breadth logging, a few GPU-days, curve shape is visible immediately.

one_line: Adapting only the text tower recovers most of dense-adaptation gains, indicating vision features are already dense-sufficient and the mismatch lives on the language side.
problem: Dense adaptation defaults to modifying the vision pathway (adapters, decoders), assuming visual features are the deficient component.
core_hypothesis: At matched trainable-parameter budgets, text-side-only adaptation (query embeddings, text adapters) achieves a large fraction of the improvement of vision-side adaptation for open-vocabulary dense tasks, because the binding constraint is aligning queries to already-present visual structure.
falsifiable_prediction: A three-way comparison (text-only, vision-only, both) at matched budgets will show text-only capturing most of the achievable gain, with the residual concentrated on boundary quality rather than region identity.
why_important: Text-side adaptation is orders of magnitude cheaper and preserves the vision tower for other tasks; if sufficient, it changes the default recipe.
why_possibly_novel: Adapter-placement studies exist for classification; a budget-matched tower-attribution study for dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the three adapter configurations at matched budgets on one dense benchmark from one frozen VLM; decompose gains into region-identity and boundary components.
main_risk: Results may depend on how much the dense domain's imagery differs from pretraining imagery; both near- and far-domain benchmarks are needed.
community_default_belief: Dense tasks need vision-side capacity: features must change to support pixels, so vision adapters are the essential ingredient.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Frozen-feature probing already shows substantial dense information present; what is missing may be queries that address it, a text-side problem.
fastest_falsification: Matched-budget adapter comparison on one benchmark, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Conclusions that VLMs 'lack localization ability' are probe artifacts: nonparametric decoders extract far more spatial information from frozen features than the linear probes used to write off the models.
problem: Claims about what frozen VLM features contain are mediated by probe choice, and the field's default (linear probing) may systematically understate spatially distributed information.
core_hypothesis: Dense information in VLM features is present but non-linearly and non-locally coded, so retrieval-based and attention-readout decoders reveal substantially better localization than linear probes at matched supervision, changing several published capability conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: Across probe families at matched label budgets, the linear-versus-nonparametric gap will be much larger for VLM features than for dense-supervised features, indicating coding format rather than information absence.
why_important: Capability conclusions steer pretraining investments; artifact-driven pessimism about contrastive pretraining would misdirect the field.
why_possibly_novel: Probe-sensitivity is a known caveat; a systematic probe-family comparison targeted at dense VLM capability claims may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate linear, MLP, retrieval, and attention-readout probes on frozen features of one VLM and one dense-supervised baseline at matched supervision on one benchmark.
main_risk: More powerful probes blur the line between reading out and learning anew; supervision-matched controls and probe-capacity accounting are essential.
community_default_belief: Linear probing is the fair standard for measuring what a representation contains.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Linearity is an arbitrary readout convention; information coded in pairwise feature relations is invisible to it yet cheaply available to retrieval decoders.
fastest_falsification: Retrieval-probe versus linear-probe comparison on cached features, a day.

one_line: Weight-space interpolation between a pretrained VLM and its dense-finetuned child traces a better breadth-versus-density tradeoff than joint multi-task training.
problem: Preserving open-vocabulary breadth while gaining dense skill is usually attempted with joint objectives, which are expensive and unstable to tune.
core_hypothesis: The pretrained and dense-finetuned weights are linearly connected with low loss barriers for both objectives, so post-hoc interpolation offers a free family of tradeoff models, some strictly dominating jointly trained baselines on the breadth-density Pareto front.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the interpolation coefficient will produce a smooth tradeoff curve, and at least one interpolated model will match the joint baseline's dense accuracy while exceeding its breadth.
why_important: A zero-training deployment knob for the field's central tradeoff, plus evidence about the loss-landscape geometry of dense finetuning.
why_possibly_novel: Weight interpolation is established for classification robustness; its systematic evaluation for the dense-breadth tradeoff may be less explored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Finetune one VLM densely; sweep interpolation; evaluate breadth and dense metrics; compare the front against one joint-training baseline at matched compute.
main_risk: Interpolation can fail for finetunes involving added modules (decoders), restricting the method to shared-backbone weights.
community_default_belief: Averaging weights between models trained for different tasks produces broken intermediate models; tradeoffs require joint optimization.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Finetuning from a shared initialization typically stays in a connected low-loss basin, making the linear path usable rather than broken.
fastest_falsification: Interpolation sweep needs only existing checkpoints and evaluation passes, a day.

one_line: Dense adaptation has a qualitatively higher LoRA-rank floor than classification adaptation, revealing that dense transfer is not a low-intrinsic-dimension update.
problem: Low-rank adaptation folklore ('tiny rank suffices') comes from classification and text tasks and is applied to dense adaptation without revalidation.
core_hypothesis: The intrinsic dimensionality of the update needed for dense tasks (which must alter spatial feature structure, not just class boundaries) is fundamentally higher, so dense accuracy saturates at much higher ranks and low-rank runs silently sacrifice boundary quality first.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank sweeps on matched backbones will show classification saturating at small ranks while segmentation continues improving to much larger ranks, with the deficit at low rank concentrated in boundary metrics.
why_important: Wrong rank defaults waste either quality (too low) or memory (too high) across thousands of dense finetuning runs; a task-dependent floor changes practice.
why_possibly_novel: Rank studies exist per task in isolation; a controlled cross-task intrinsic-dimensionality comparison with error-anatomy analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: LoRA rank sweep on one VLM for one classification and one segmentation task, matched optimization budgets; record saturation ranks and boundary-versus-interior error anatomy.
main_risk: Saturation rank depends on layer placement of LoRA, requiring the sweep to cover placement as a secondary factor.
community_default_belief: A small LoRA rank captures almost all of finetuning's benefit regardless of the downstream task.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Class-boundary updates are few-directional; reshaping spatial feature geometry across positions plausibly requires many more directions.
fastest_falsification: Two-task rank sweep at three ranks each, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Distilling a VLM into a dense specialist preserves open-vocabulary breadth better than finetuning the VLM itself, at matched dense accuracy.
problem: The standard route to a dense VLM is finetuning the foundation model, accepting breadth loss as inevitable; distillation as the primary adaptation mechanism is under-considered.
core_hypothesis: Keeping the VLM frozen as a teacher and distilling its patch-text affinities into a student dense architecture avoids touching the alignment that finetuning damages, yielding a better breadth-density operating point than direct finetuning at matched compute.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched dense-benchmark accuracy, the distilled student plus frozen teacher pipeline will retain substantially more held-out-vocabulary performance than the finetuned VLM.
why_important: If distillation dominates, the ecosystem's default adaptation recipe is wrong, and foundation-model weights should be treated as read-only assets.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation for open-vocabulary detection exists; the explicit breadth-preservation comparison against finetuning at matched dense accuracy may be underexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build one distilled student and one finetuned VLM from the same teacher at matched compute; evaluate both on dense accuracy and held-out vocabulary breadth.
main_risk: Students inherit teacher errors and add capacity limits; matched-compute bookkeeping across such different pipelines is delicate.
community_default_belief: Finetuning the foundation model is the strongest adaptation route; distillation is a compression afterthought.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Finetuning pays an unpriced cost (alignment damage) that distillation structurally avoids by never writing to the teacher.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale paired comparison on one benchmark with one held-out vocabulary suite, several GPU-days.

one_line: Paraphrase robustness collapses before seen-prompt accuracy during dense finetuning, providing an early-warning metric for alignment damage.
problem: Practitioners monitor dense accuracy and perhaps seen-class zero-shot performance during finetuning, missing the earliest signs of text-alignment degradation.
core_hypothesis: Finetuning first destroys the text encoder's local semantic smoothness: performance under paraphrased prompts diverges from canonical-prompt performance well before canonical-prompt metrics move, so paraphrase-gap tracking predicts eventual breadth loss early enough to intervene.
falsifiable_prediction: During dense finetuning, the paraphrase gap (canonical minus paraphrase performance) will widen significantly earlier in training than any decline in canonical zero-shot metrics, and its early slope will predict final breadth loss across runs.
why_important: An early-warning signal makes breadth preservation an engineering practice (stop, freeze, or regularize when the alarm fires) instead of a post-mortem discovery.
why_possibly_novel: Paraphrase robustness is studied statically; its use as a leading indicator during dense finetuning may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument one finetuning run with frequent paraphrase-gap and canonical-metric evaluations; test lead-lag structure; replicate across two learning rates.
main_risk: Paraphrase sets must be validated as meaning-preserving, or the gap measures paraphrase quality instead of model smoothness.
community_default_belief: Monitoring canonical zero-shot metrics during finetuning suffices to detect forgetting when it matters.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Canonical prompts are the last thing to break because finetuning data keeps reinforcing their neighborhood; the semantic neighborhood decays first and invisibly.
fastest_falsification: Add paraphrase evaluation to an existing finetuning script and re-run one training, days.

one_line: A large share of cross-domain dense-transfer loss in VLM pipelines is normalization-statistics mismatch, recoverable by recomputing norm statistics without any gradient training.
problem: Domain shift for dense VLM systems is met with finetuning or domain adaptation pipelines, skipping the cheapest hypothesis: the normalization layers are mis-calibrated for the new domain's activation statistics.
core_hypothesis: Recomputing or re-estimating normalization statistics (and only those) on unlabeled target-domain images recovers a substantial fraction of the dense performance lost to domain shift, with the recoverable fraction predictable from the activation-statistics divergence between domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Across several target domains, norm-statistics adaptation will recover a consistent, non-trivial share of the frozen-model-to-finetuned-model gap, and the share will correlate with measured activation divergence.
why_important: A label-free, gradient-free, minutes-scale adaptation step would change deployment practice for every cross-domain dense application.
why_possibly_novel: Norm adaptation is known for CNN classification under corruption; its systematic evaluation for VLM dense transfer with a predictive divergence measure may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one segmenter and three shifted domains, compare frozen, norm-adapted, and finetuned variants; regress recovery share on activation divergence.
main_risk: Transformer LayerNorm has no batch statistics to swap, so the method needs care (adapting affine parameters or inserted rescaling), which weakens the 'zero-training' framing.
community_default_belief: Meaningful domain adaptation requires gradient-based training on target-domain data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the representation is domain-robust but its per-layer scaling is not, the failure is a units problem, not a knowledge problem.
fastest_falsification: Norm recalibration on one shifted benchmark, under a day including evaluation.

one_line: Attribute-object binding fails at pixel level in predictable directions: dense models swap attributes between instances rather than failing randomly.
problem: Binding failures ('red cup next to blue book' grounding red to the book) are demonstrated for retrieval and generation, but their dense-output structure is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: When multiple attribute-bearing instances are present, dense predictions exhibit structured swaps (attributes migrate to the more salient or larger instance) rather than uniform noise, and swap direction is predicted by a saliency-asymmetry score computable from the image alone.
falsifiable_prediction: On controlled two-object scenes, binding errors will concentrate in the swap configuration far above chance, and a saliency-asymmetry predictor will forecast swap direction significantly better than random.
why_important: Structured errors are exploitable (post-hoc correction, targeted training) while random errors are not; knowing the structure changes the mitigation strategy.
why_possibly_novel: Binding is a known weakness; the dense-level swap-structure characterization with a predictive image-side score may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or render two-object attribute scenes with controlled saliency; evaluate referring queries per attribute-object combination; tabulate error configurations against the predictor.
main_risk: Rendered scenes may understate real-world binding difficulty or introduce distributional artifacts.
community_default_belief: Compositional failures are diffuse noise reflecting general model weakness, without exploitable structure.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Bag-of-words matching plus saliency weighting mechanically produces directional swaps, so structure is expected, not surprising.
fastest_falsification: A few hundred controlled scenes on one model, one day including rendering.
