one_line: Pixel-level attribute binding degrades sharply with instance count, following a capacity-like scaling law in scene complexity that current benchmarks never probe.
problem: Binding evaluations use two-object scenes; real scenes contain many attribute-bearing instances, and the degradation law is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Binding accuracy per instance falls faster than linearly as attribute-bearing instance count grows, consistent with interference in superposed feature representations, and the collapse point is architecture-dependent (cross-attention systems degrade more gracefully than pooled-similarity systems).
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy-versus-instance-count curves will show super-linear per-instance degradation with an architecture-dependent knee, and the ordering of architectures by knee position will be consistent across attribute types.
why_important: It defines the operating envelope of dense VLM systems for cluttered real-world scenes and gives architecture designers a measurable target.
why_possibly_novel: Set-size effects are studied in cognitive science and VQA counting; a dense binding scaling-law analysis across architectures may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Procedurally generate scenes sweeping instance count with controlled attributes; evaluate two architecture families; fit degradation curves.
main_risk: Procedural scenes risk low visual realism; a smaller real-image validation subset is needed to anchor conclusions.
community_default_belief: A model that binds attributes in demonstration scenes has 'solved binding' for practical purposes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interference effects are invisible at small set sizes by construction; the practical regime is exactly where evaluation is missing.
fastest_falsification: Instance-count sweep with rendered scenes on one system, days.

one_line: Attribute information in VLM features is channel-sparse: a few feature directions carry color/material/state, and causal edits to them flip dense predictions.
problem: Whether attributes are encoded diffusely or in localized feature subspaces determines what interventions (editing, debiasing, binding fixes) are possible, and for dense VLM features it is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Linear attribute directions identified on patch features generalize across categories and positions, and intervening on them (projection removal, direction addition) changes attribute-conditioned dense predictions in the predicted direction without disturbing category predictions, demonstrating sparse, manipulable attribute coding.
falsifiable_prediction: Attribute-direction interventions will flip attribute-conditioned mask assignments in a large fraction of cases while leaving category-only queries nearly unchanged, and the same directions will work across object categories.
why_important: Sparse attribute coding would enable surgical fixes for binding and bias problems without retraining, and inform how compositional queries should be executed.
why_possibly_novel: Concept directions are studied for classification interpretability; causal direction-editing evaluated on dense outputs may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Learn attribute directions from labeled patches; apply interventions on held-out images; measure attribute-query flip rates and category-query stability for one segmenter.
main_risk: Directions may be entangled with correlated attributes (red with warm lighting), making 'surgical' edits leaky.
community_default_belief: Attribute information in deep features is distributed and only manipulable through finetuning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive alignment to compositional text plausibly factorizes attributes into near-linear structure, as it does for word embeddings.
fastest_falsification: Direction fitting and intervention on cached features, one day.

one_line: Dense VLM systems treat relational prompts as conjunctions: 'A on B' produces the same masks as 'A and B', measurable as relation-invariance.
problem: Relational queries are assumed to constrain dense outputs through the relation, but systems may only extract the noun set.
core_hypothesis: Predicted masks for relational prompts are statistically indistinguishable from conjunction prompts with identical nouns, across relation types and systems built on contrastive text towers, whereas LLM-decoder systems show partial but incomplete relation sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask agreement between relational and conjunction prompts will approach paraphrase-level agreement for contrastive systems, and relation-conditioned accuracy will not exceed a noun-only baseline.
why_important: It defines what query complexity is actually executable by current architectures, preventing overclaiming in applications that rely on relational filtering.
why_possibly_novel: Relation insensitivity is suspected from retrieval studies; a dense-output relational-versus-conjunction equivalence test across architecture families may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired relational/conjunction prompts on scenes where the relation selects a strict subset; measure mask agreement and subset-selection accuracy for two architecture families.
main_risk: Scenes where relations select strict subsets need careful curation; leakage from object priors can mask relation use.
community_default_belief: Modern grounded VLMs execute the full query semantics, including relations, when producing masks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the query representation collapses to a bag of nouns before touching pixels, relations are lost upstream of grounding, whatever the decoder does.
fastest_falsification: Agreement analysis on paired prompts, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Part-whole queries fail asymmetrically: 'the wheel of the car' returns whole-car masks, and part grounding quality is predicted by the part's caption-mention rate, not its visual size.
problem: Part segmentation through language is increasingly demanded (robotics affordances, editing), but VLM behavior on part queries is uncharacterized beyond anecdote.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictions for part queries are biased toward the containing whole, with the bias strength inversely related to how often the part is independently captioned in web text; frequently captioned parts (face, wheel) ground well while rarely captioned parts (hinge, cuff) collapse to wholes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a part-query battery, whole-mask leakage will correlate negatively with caption-mention frequency of the part word, controlling for part pixel area.
why_important: Parts are where dense language interfaces meet manipulation and editing; knowing which parts are queryable and why enables vocabulary design and targeted data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Part segmentation datasets exist; the caption-frequency explanation of part-query failure in VLM systems may be untested; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a part-query battery over a part-annotated dataset; measure whole-leakage per part; regress on caption frequency and area.
main_risk: Part annotations vary in granularity conventions across datasets, complicating leakage measurement.
community_default_belief: Part queries are just smaller-object queries; performance tracks visual difficulty of the part.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A part that is never a caption subject has no text anchor of its own, making it invisible to text-driven grounding regardless of visual clarity.
fastest_falsification: Part battery on one part-annotated benchmark, inference plus regression, a day.

one_line: Training with programmatically recombined captions improves pixel-level binding but measurably degrades rare-noun grounding, a compositionality-versus-coverage tradeoff nobody reports.
problem: Compositional augmentation (shuffling attributes and objects into new captions) is a popular fix for binding, evaluated only on binding metrics.
core_hypothesis: Recombined captions inject distributional noise for rare nouns (attaching them to atypical contexts), so binding gains come with a hidden tax on rare-vocabulary dense performance; the tradeoff is tunable by restricting recombination to frequent nouns.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with aggressive recombination will improve on binding batteries while dropping on rare-class dense metrics relative to identically budgeted baselines, and frequency-restricted recombination will recover most of the drop.
why_important: Data-augmentation recipes propagate rapidly; an unreported side effect on the open-vocabulary tail would silently damage exactly what these models are prized for.
why_possibly_novel: Compositional augmentation is studied for binding gains; its interaction with vocabulary-tail performance may be unexamined; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with none/full/frequency-restricted recombination; evaluate binding and frequency-stratified dense metrics.
main_risk: The effect may depend on augmentation ratio, requiring a sweep to characterize rather than a single comparison.
community_default_belief: Compositional augmentation is a free lunch: it fixes binding without costing anything measurable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Any augmentation reshapes the training distribution; for tail nouns whose few examples are their entire signal, reshaping is expensive.
fastest_falsification: Two small matched training runs with the stratified evaluation suite, several GPU-days.

one_line: A dense analogue of minimal-pair compositional benchmarks will show VLM dense systems near chance on composition even when their global image-text matching succeeds.
problem: Minimal-pair compositional evaluation exists for retrieval, but dense prediction lacks an equivalent, so compositional claims about grounded systems rest on unsuitable aggregate metrics.
core_hypothesis: On minimal pairs distinguishable only by composition (same objects and attributes, different binding or relation), dense systems will assign masks at near-chance consistency with the intended reading, and their dense compositional score will be uncorrelated with their retrieval-level compositional score, showing the two abilities dissociate.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense minimal-pair accuracy will hover near chance for most systems, and cross-system correlation between dense and retrieval compositional scores will be weak.
why_important: It gives the field a targeted instrument for measuring grounded compositionality, separating it from image-level matching heuristics.
why_possibly_novel: Retrieval minimal-pair benchmarks are established; a dense-output minimal-pair protocol with the dissociation analysis may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a modest dense minimal-pair suite from staged photos or renders; evaluate several systems on dense and retrieval versions; test the correlation.
main_risk: Constructing truly minimal visual pairs is laborious, and residual low-level differences can leak the answer.
community_default_belief: Grounded systems that pass retrieval compositional tests will also compose correctly at pixel level, since grounding is stricter.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Retrieval success can come from global co-occurrence heuristics that never resolve which pixels bind to which words; strictness is assumed, not demonstrated.
fastest_falsification: A pilot suite of a few dozen pairs on two systems, days including staging.

one_line: Non-English prompts degrade dense prediction disproportionately relative to classification, because pixel-level matching amplifies text-embedding quality differences.
problem: Multilingual capability of VLMs is certified on classification or retrieval, and dense multilingual behavior is assumed to follow, without measurement.
core_hypothesis: Dense tasks compound per-query embedding error across thousands of pixel decisions, so the multilingual performance gap (relative to English) will be systematically larger for segmentation/detection than for classification on matched concepts, and largest for low-resource languages.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring English-relative performance ratios per language, dense tasks will show consistently lower ratios than classification for the same model and concepts, with the deficit ordered by language resource level.
why_important: Global deployments assume multilingual parity certified at image level; a dense-specific multilingual tax would mislead exactly the users least able to debug it.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual VLM audits exist for retrieval/classification; the dense-versus-global degradation comparison may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Translate one benchmark's class names into several languages of varying resource level; evaluate one multilingual VLM on classification and segmentation with matched vocabularies; compare degradation ratios.
main_risk: Translation quality itself varies by language, requiring native-speaker validation of class-name translations.
community_default_belief: A multilingual text tower gives language-independent dense capability; the vision side does the spatial work.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dense outputs are equilibria of many small text-vision comparisons, so small per-comparison embedding degradations accumulate rather than average out.
fastest_falsification: Two-language pilot (one high-resource, one low-resource) on one benchmark, inference-only, a day.

one_line: In specialist domains, rewriting class names into web-vernacular lay terms rivals vision-side finetuning for open-vocabulary dense performance.
problem: Medical, aerial, and industrial vocabularies use terminology absent from web captions, and the default fix is expensive vision-side domain finetuning.
core_hypothesis: Much of the domain gap is a query-language gap: specialist terms embed poorly while the underlying visual patterns are within the model's reach, so translating vocabularies into caption-style descriptions ('ground-glass opacity' to a lay visual description) recovers a large fraction of finetuning's gain at zero training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: On specialist dense benchmarks, vocabulary rewriting will close a substantial fraction of the frozen-to-finetuned gap, and the per-class recovery will correlate with how far the original term is from the caption distribution.
why_important: It would replace an expensive, per-domain training pipeline with a prompt-engineering step accessible to non-ML domain experts.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt rewriting is common practice; its quantitative benchmarking against vision finetuning on specialist dense tasks may be missing; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one medical and one aerial benchmark, compare frozen + original names, frozen + rewritten names, and lightly finetuned models; attribute the gap closure.
main_risk: Some specialist classes have no adequate lay description, capping the method's coverage.
community_default_belief: Specialist domains require domain-trained vision features; prompt wording cannot bridge a domain gap.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The vision tower has seen vast natural-image diversity that may cover specialist appearances; what it has never seen is the jargon.
fastest_falsification: Rewrite one benchmark's vocabulary with a domain expert or LLM assistance and re-evaluate frozen performance, a day.

one_line: For non-photographic imagery (thermal, ultrasound, sketches), VLM dense failure is vision-encoder-side, not text-side, and the attribution is measurable by asymmetric substitution.
problem: When VLM dense prediction fails on non-photographic modalities, pipelines cannot tell whether to fix the vision encoder, the text prompts, or both.
core_hypothesis: Substituting a modality-adapted vision encoder (while keeping original text queries) recovers far more dense performance than any text-side intervention (rewriting, ensembling) on the frozen original encoder, establishing that the modality gap lives almost entirely in vision feature extraction.
falsifiable_prediction: In a substitution matrix (original/adapted vision crossed with original/optimized text), the vision axis will explain the large majority of performance variance on non-photographic dense benchmarks.
why_important: It directs scarce adaptation budgets to the right tower and quantifies a decomposition tool reusable across modalities.
why_possibly_novel: Modality-gap studies exist at embedding level; the causal substitution-matrix attribution for dense tasks may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble the two-by-two substitution matrix for one thermal or sketch dense benchmark; measure variance explained by each axis.
main_risk: Building a fairly 'adapted' vision encoder without leaking dense supervision requires discipline; self-supervised adaptation on unlabeled target imagery is the clean choice.
community_default_belief: Both towers degrade together off-distribution, so full-pipeline finetuning is the necessary response.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Class names for these domains (person, tumor, chair) are ordinary words the text tower handles fine; only the pixels are alien.
fastest_falsification: Text-side-optimization-only versus vision-swap-only comparison on one benchmark, days.

one_line: Open-vocabulary dense performance varies geographically for the same class, tracking the geographic distribution of captioned imagery rather than visual difficulty.
problem: Classes like 'house', 'market', or 'stove' look different across regions, and dense models trained on geographically skewed captions may ground the concept's dominant-region appearance only.
core_hypothesis: Per-region dense performance for common classes correlates with estimated regional representation in caption corpora, after controlling for image quality and scene clutter, revealing a geographic fairness gap specific to the open-vocabulary mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: On geographically annotated imagery, region-stratified dense metrics will show gaps aligned with corpus representation estimates, larger for culturally variable classes than for globally uniform ones (car versus stove).
why_important: Dense systems are deployed globally (mapping, humanitarian response); a geographic performance gradient is a concrete fairness and reliability issue.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic bias is documented for classification; the dense-prediction extension with corpus-representation correlation may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one open-vocabulary segmenter on a geographically diverse annotated set; stratify by region and class cultural-variability; correlate with representation proxies.
main_risk: Region-stratified dense annotations are scarce; may require targeted annotation of an existing geo-diverse image collection.
community_default_belief: A class is a class: open-vocabulary models generalize across appearance variation within a category.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text anchor is shared, but the visual cluster it points to is the caption-weighted average, which is geographically skewed.
fastest_falsification: Region-stratified evaluation on any available geo-tagged annotated subset, analysis within days.

one_line: In unfamiliar visual domains, VLM dense grounding falls back to texture words over shape words, re-expressing the texture bias at the language-grounding level.
problem: When domain shift breaks learned category associations, it is unknown which linguistic cues (shape terms versus texture/material terms) retain grounding power.
core_hypothesis: Out of distribution, queries built from texture and material words will localize regions substantially better than queries built from shape words, mirroring the classic texture bias but now measurable through the language interface, and implying that OOD vocabulary design should prefer material descriptions.
falsifiable_prediction: On cue-conflict and OOD dense probes, texture-word queries will outperform shape-word queries by a margin much larger than their in-domain difference.
why_important: It yields immediately actionable vocabulary-design guidance for OOD deployments and connects the texture-bias literature to the grounding interface.
why_possibly_novel: Texture bias is established for classification; its manifestation in text-query dense grounding may be uncharted; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched shape-word and texture-word query sets for objects in an OOD domain; compare dense localization quality per query type in and out of domain.
main_risk: Shape and texture words differ in frequency and specificity; matching query informativeness across the two sets is the hard part.
community_default_belief: Shape is the more robust cue, so shape-based descriptions should generalize better out of domain.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The vision tower's features may encode texture more transferably than shape, making the text anchor's robustness irrelevant if the visual cluster it addresses dissolves.
fastest_falsification: Matched query battery on one OOD dense dataset, inference-only, a day.

one_line: Code-switched prompts (mixed-language queries) break dense grounding disproportionately, exposing tokenizer-level fragility invisible in single-language evaluations.
problem: Real multilingual users mix languages within queries ('segment the coche on the left'), a regime absent from all dense evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Code-switching fragments tokenization and pushes query embeddings off both languages' manifolds, so dense performance under code-switched prompts falls below the worse of the two single-language conditions, rather than between them as a smooth-interpolation view would predict.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense metrics under code-switched prompts will be significantly below the minimum of the corresponding single-language conditions, and the drop will correlate with tokenization fragmentation measures of the mixed query.
why_important: Sub-minimum behavior means multilingual certification via per-language testing overstates real-world robustness for the many users who code-switch naturally.
why_possibly_novel: Code-switching is studied in NLP; its effect on dense visual grounding may be unexamined; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct code-switched variants of referring expressions in two language pairs; evaluate one multilingual dense system against both single-language baselines; test the sub-minimum prediction.
main_risk: Naturalistic code-switching follows grammatical patterns; artificial mixtures may exaggerate the effect, so templates need native-speaker construction.
community_default_belief: A multilingual model's performance on mixed input interpolates between its single-language performances.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interpolation assumes the mixture stays on the training distribution; code-switched text may be off-manifold for caption-trained encoders, making the mixture worse than its parts.
fastest_falsification: Small code-switched battery for one language pair, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Referring-segmentation benchmarks are largely solvable from the head noun plus saliency, so modifier-ablated evaluation is needed to measure actual referring ability.
problem: High benchmark scores are read as evidence of expression understanding, but most benchmark expressions may be resolvable without reading past the head noun.
core_hypothesis: Ablating all modifiers from referring expressions (keeping only the head noun) preserves the large majority of benchmark accuracy for top systems, meaning the benchmarks mostly test open-vocabulary object detection, and true referring skill is concentrated in (and measurable on) the small expression subset where ablation hurts.
falsifiable_prediction: Head-noun-only accuracy will be a large fraction of full-expression accuracy for several top systems, and cross-model ranking on the ablation-sensitive subset will differ from the full-benchmark ranking.
why_important: If the metric mostly measures detection, progress claims about language understanding in grounding are misdirected, and the sensitive subset becomes the real benchmark.
why_possibly_novel: Ablation analyses exist in pockets; using ablation sensitivity to redefine the effective benchmark and re-rank systems may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three systems on one referring benchmark with full and head-noun-only expressions; compute preservation ratios and subset re-rankings.
main_risk: Automatic head-noun extraction errors could contaminate the ablation; manual verification on a sample is needed.
community_default_belief: Referring benchmarks measure the integration of language constraints with visual grounding.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dataset construction favored unambiguous referents, which mechanically makes modifiers redundant and the language component optional.
fastest_falsification: Head-noun ablation on one system, inference-only, hours.

one_line: Correction turns ('no, the other one') fail in dense VLM systems because nothing represents the rejected hypothesis, and a minimal exclusion memory fixes a large fraction of failures.
problem: Interactive segmentation with language assumes users can repair errors conversationally, but architectures process each turn statelessly at the grounding level.
core_hypothesis: On correction turns, current systems re-predict their first choice at high rates (having no representation of 'not that one'), and augmenting inference with an explicit exclusion constraint (suppress the previously returned instance) recovers most correction-turn failures without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured repeat-error rate on correction turns will be far above chance, and the exclusion-augmented variant will cut it dramatically while leaving first-turn behavior unchanged.
why_important: Correction is the core interaction loop of practical dense tools; a stateless loop that repeats its mistake is unusable regardless of first-shot accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive segmentation studies clicks extensively; language-correction statefulness and the minimal exclusion fix may be unexplored; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a two-turn protocol from existing benchmarks (first query, then a templated correction); measure repeat rates for two systems with and without exclusion augmentation.
main_risk: Templated corrections may not represent natural correction language, though the stateless failure mode should be phrasing-independent.
community_default_belief: Stronger language models in the loop will handle dialog phenomena like corrections without architectural changes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Understanding the correction linguistically does not help if the grounding pathway has no channel to receive and apply an exclusion.
fastest_falsification: Two-turn repeat-rate measurement on one system, one day.

one_line: Speaker-relative referring expressions in egocentric video are systematically grounded in the camera frame, a specific and correctable perspective bug.
problem: Assistive and robotic systems consume expressions from speakers whose viewpoint differs from the camera's, a mismatch dense grounding systems are never tested on.
core_hypothesis: When a visible speaker says 'the cup on my left', dense systems resolve 'left' in the camera frame at rates far above chance, ignoring the possessive frame marker; injecting an estimated speaker pose as a coordinate transform on the query fixes the majority of such errors without retraining the grounder.
falsifiable_prediction: On stimuli where camera and speaker frames disagree, camera-frame groundings will dominate errors, and the pose-transform augmentation will flip most of them to correct.
why_important: Perspective-taking is mandatory for any embodied assistant; a characterized, modular fix is more deployable than end-to-end retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Perspective-taking is studied in embodied AI simulations; the dense-grounding failure characterization with a modular pose-transform fix may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate egocentric clips with visible speakers and frame-disambiguating referents; evaluate one grounding system raw and with pose-transform query rewriting.
main_risk: Speaker pose estimation errors propagate into the fix, potentially trading one systematic error for another.
community_default_belief: Frame-of-reference errors are rare edge cases that scale and instruction tuning will wash out.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training data almost never labels speaker-relative frames, so no amount of scale provides the missing supervision signal.
fastest_falsification: A small curated clip set with paired-frame prompts on one system, days including curation.

one_line: Beyond their information content, longer referring expressions actively hurt dense grounding: added words dilute attention rather than adding constraints.
problem: Users and prompt engineers assume more descriptive expressions help the model; the marginal effect of expression length at fixed information content is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed referent and fixed disambiguating information, padding expressions with redundant true details reduces grounding accuracy monotonically, because pooled or cross-attended text representations dilute the discriminative tokens; the effect is stronger in contrastive-tower systems than LLM-decoder systems.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy versus expression length at matched information content will show a negative slope, steeper for pooled-text architectures, and token-attribution analysis will show discriminative-token weight shrinking as length grows.
why_important: It contradicts universal prompt-writing advice for grounding tasks and gives users a concrete instruction: say less, but say the distinguishing thing.
why_possibly_novel: Length effects are studied for retrieval and LLM prompts; a controlled information-matched length study for dense grounding may be new; not verified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct expression sets per referent sweeping length with verified-constant disambiguating content; evaluate two architecture families; fit the length-accuracy slope.
main_risk: Holding information content truly constant while varying length is linguistically delicate and needs human validation.
community_default_belief: Richer, longer descriptions give grounding models more to work with and can only help disambiguation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fixed-capacity query representations must share mass across tokens, so every redundant word is paid for by the words that mattered.
fastest_falsification: Length-sweep battery for a few dozen referents on one system, inference-only, a day.
